findings.paper_title: DFP-26-73 Internal Audit Annual Report June 2026
findings.headline: Large employer compliance backlog indicates sustained operational pressure
findings.detail: The Fund accumulated over 1,400 outstanding employer data cases by May 2025. A chasing process implemented in June 2025 reduced this to 199 by January 2026—substantial progress, but the size of the backlog that built up and the ongoing cases suggest chronic employer engagement difficulties. Only 14 employers have been fined since the enforcement process began despite strategy allowing for fines.
findings.matters: A backlog this large indicates the Fund has struggled to enforce compliance with employers. This reflects operational control weakness and suggests the Fund may have limited leverage over employers or faces systematic non-compliance.
findings.figures: Outstanding cases: 1,400+ in May 2025 → 199 in January 2026; 14 employers fined to date
findings.quote: The process has resulted in improved employer responsiveness and a significant reduction in outstanding cases, from over 1,400 in May 2025 to 199 in January 2026.

findings.paper_title: DFP-26-73 Internal Audit Annual Report June 2026
findings.headline: Pension Administration Strategy compliance procedures do not align with published timescales
findings.detail: The formal employer chasing process for outstanding data, introduced June 2025, allows employers three months to provide information. This does not match Appendix C of the Pension Admin Strategies. The extended timescale was a temporary measure during rollout and will be realigned from April 2026. This misalignment between actual operating procedures and documented policy suggests control framework gaps.
findings.matters: Documented procedures that do not match actual practice indicate control framework weaknesses and create risk that governance reporting may not reflect reality. A finance director needs to know that published procedures are actually being followed.
findings.figures: Three-month timescale currently applied; realignment planned April 2026
findings.quote: While the process is operating effectively, the timescales currently applied, which allows employers three months to provide outstanding information, does not align with Appendix C of the Strategies. This extended timescale was a temporary measure to support employers during the initial roll out when there was a high number of outstanding cases. Peninsula Pensions has confirmed that the process will be brought into alignment with the Strategies from April 2026.

findings.paper_title: DFP-26-73 Internal Audit Annual Report June 2026
findings.headline: Data quality control weakness persists: nearly 1 in 5 employers' pension contributions cannot be verified
findings.detail: Internal audit could not verify the accuracy of pension contribution data for 9 out of 46 employers sampled (19%) due to employer non-engagement or failure to provide supporting information. Devon accounted for 2 out of 27 employers (7%) and Somerset 4 out of 19 (21%). Critically, this rate has not improved from the previous audit in May 2025 (which reported 20%), indicating a persistent and unresolved control gap.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the Fund's financial position must have confidence that contribution data is accurate—these are the inputs to calculating pension liabilities and member benefits. When the Fund cannot verify data for nearly 1 in 5 employers, the accuracy of its overall financial position and liability calculations is unreliable.
findings.figures: 9 out of 46 employers (19%) could not be verified; Devon 2/27 (7%); Somerset 4/19 (21%); unchanged from May 2025 (20%)
findings.quote: Auditor not being able to verify the accuracy of data for nine employers (19%) of our sample, primarily through non-engagement, or not providing the correct data. This compares to 20% as reported at the previous audit in May 2025.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Devon County Council County Fund Balance and Earmarked Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: Public Health Reserve is being drawn down for ongoing service costs, declining from £10.8m to £2m by March 2031
findings.detail: The Public Health Reserve, which was £10.784m at March 2026, is forecast to decline to £2.021m by March 2031. The council plans to use £1.7m in 2026/27, £2.7m in 2027/28, £1.5m in 2028/29 and 2029/30. This pattern suggests ongoing Public Health service costs are not fully funded from revenue budget and require reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund ongoing operational costs (not one-off spending) is a sign that the revenue base may not cover current service commitments. It reduces reserve flexibility for genuine emergencies or unexpected costs.
findings.figures: Public Health Reserve: £10,784k (March 2026), declining to £2,021k (March 2031); planned annual spend: £1,700k, £2,700k, £1,500k, £1,500k
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget anticipates use of just under £1.7 million of the Public Health reserve in 2026/27 and just over £2.7 million in 2027/28 and just over £1.5 million 2028/29 and 2029/30 to meet relevant service costs each year.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Devon County Council County Fund Balance and Earmarked Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: Transfer of £41.7m SEND Resilience Reserve to Budget Management Reserve depends on Department for Education confirmation of future deficit support arrangements
findings.detail: The council set aside £41.7m as a Resilience Reserve for SEND under the now-ending Safety Valve program. This will be transferred to Budget Management Reserve to increase resilience, but the document states 'Further details of how this will operate in practice are expected to follow, the MTFP and reserves strategy will be updated once more information is known.' This means the reserve plan may need to be revised depending on DfE guidance.
findings.matters: A £41.7m reserve movement contingent on unconfirmed government policy creates planning uncertainty. If DfE expectations differ from current assumptions, the reserve position could change materially.
findings.figures: £41.7 million Resilience Reserve planned for transfer to Budget Management Reserve
findings.quote: Due to the negotiations with Government set out within the Medium Term Financial Plan this reserve is no longer needed and will, subject to budget approval, be transferred to the Budget Management Reserve while we await confirmation from the DfE on expectations of how local authorities can address the DSG deficit not funded by the High Needs Stability Grant.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Devon County Council County Fund Balance and Earmarked Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: SEND accumulated deficit of £221.5m is the council's single largest financial risk; local contribution required totals £42.5m despite 90% government grant
findings.detail: The council has accumulated a £221.457m deficit in its Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) budget. Government will provide the High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of historic deficits (£194.245m in Phase 1, £137.941m in Phase 2), but the council must contribute £42.539m across two phases. Crucially, support for new deficits arising in 2026/27 onwards has not yet been confirmed.
findings.matters: A £221m accumulated liability, even partially grant-funded, is a material liability. The residual £42.5m local contribution is large enough to constrain other spending or require reserve drawdowns. The lack of confirmed support for future years' deficits creates ongoing uncertainty about council finances.
findings.figures: Estimated Cumulative DSG deficit at 1 April 2026: £221,457k; Local contribution Phase 1: £27,212k; Local contribution Phase 2: £15,327k; Total: £42,539k
findings.quote: The single largest financial risk to the authority remains the DSG SEND cumulative deficit.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Devon County Council County Fund Balance and Earmarked Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: External auditor issued a formal improvement recommendation to protect and strengthen reserve levels
findings.detail: Grant Thornton, the council's external auditor, made an Improvement Recommendation (IR1) in its 2024/25 Value for Money Audit. The recommendation requires the council to review whether the minimum General Fund Balance is sufficient, and to ensure that plans to increase earmarked reserves through future years are deliverable while managing in-year budget pressures.
findings.matters: An auditor improvement recommendation signals that governance bodies have identified a material area needing management attention; it flags a control or strategy weakness that the council must address.
findings.figures: IR1 recommendation from 2024/25 Value for Money Audit
findings.quote: The authority's external auditors, Grant Thornton, has made an Improvement Recommendation as part of its Value for Money Audit 2024/25. IR1: The Council should seek to protect the level of reserves and ensure that they are sufficient to provide sufficient financial resilience.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Devon County Council County Fund Balance and Earmarked Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: Reserves have declined relative to other county councils and are approaching a threshold where they would be deemed inadequate
findings.detail: The council benchmarks itself against the 21 other English county councils and has fallen behind over recent years, mainly due to government funding reductions that have made significant reserve contributions unaffordable. The document explicitly states the current level is 'close to the level where they could be deemed not to be adequate'.
findings.matters: Reserve adequacy is a core indicator of financial resilience; weak reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb shocks or unexpected costs, and lenders care about the borrower's financial buffers.
findings.figures: Current General Fund Working Balance held flat at £16,036k; General Earmarked Reserves to grow from £121,990k (March 2026) to £197,939k (March 2031) through planned contributions
findings.quote: In recent years benchmarking of reserves has shown the authority's position decline compared to other County Councils... The level of reserves held currently is close to the level where they could be deemed not to be adequate

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation has been formally recorded as a significant area of uncertainty affecting the Council's future
findings.detail: LGR is explicitly recorded on the Council's risk register as representing significant uncertainty. The Council is developing new corporate risk and controls designed to be adaptable across scenarios that could affect service delivery, to strengthen resilience in face of major disruptive events.
findings.matters: LGR represents a major structural change affecting the Council's future form, financial position, and service continuity; it creates material uncertainty relevant to lenders and the finance director.
findings.figures: None provided in paper
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) represents a significant area of uncertainty for the Council and has therefore been formally recorded on the Council's risk register

findings.headline: SEND delivery remains assessed at High risk level despite active management efforts
findings.detail: The Risk Management team maintains regular engagement with the Children and Young People's Futures service on SEND risks. The Council has delivered targeted risk management training to the Inclusion & Learning team and held leadership meetings. Recent collaboration led to refinement of risks; however, the overall SEND risk position remains at High level.
findings.matters: SEND is a high-cost, high-exposure service area where delivery failures drive budget variances and legal risk; High risk status indicates material ongoing concerns.
findings.figures: None provided in paper
findings.quote: the overall risk position remains appropriately assessed at a High level

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation outcome pending government decision July 2026 creates significant structural uncertainty
findings.detail: In response to the Government's statutory invitation in February 2025, the council submitted a business case in November 2025 for a single tier of local government across Devon meeting stated criteria. However, there is no overall agreed local government reorganisation proposal for the area. The council continues to work with other 10 local authorities on planning for Government's final decision on the structure of local government within the county, expected in July 2026. This introduces material uncertainty around the council's future structure, financial arrangements and governance.
findings.matters: Pending local government reorganisation creates fundamental uncertainty about the council's future structure, financial allocation, and service delivery model within the 2026 financial year, affecting financial planning and risk assessment.
findings.figures: Business case submitted November 2025; government decision expected July 2026
findings.quote: In response to the Government's statutory invitation in February 2025, the Council has developed a proposal for a single tier of local government across Devon submitting its business case in November 2025 that met the stated criteria. There is no overall agreed local government reorganisation proposal for the area, and the Council continues to work with the other 10 local authorities and wider stakeholders to plan for Government's final decision for the structure of local government within the county that is expected in July 2026.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care engaged external partner Newton for financial sustainability support
findings.detail: Following Cabinet approval in September 2025, Integrated Adult Social Care commenced a partnership with Newton to support delivery of improvement priorities and financial sustainability. While internal audit work provided overall reasonable assurance and the directorate achieved predominantly reasonable assurance opinions with some substantial assurance areas, the need for external partnership support suggests financial sustainability challenges within this major service area.
findings.matters: Engagement of external partners to address financial sustainability in adult social care indicates the council identified challenges it could not resolve independently, signalling material financial pressures in this large demand-led service.
findings.figures: Partnership with Newton commenced September 2025
findings.quote: IASC has commenced a partnership with Newton to support delivery of its improvement priorities and financial sustainability, with governance arrangements in place to ensure appropriate oversight, transparency and alignment with existing assurance frameworks.

findings.headline: Children's Services improvement plan needed after Ofsted found systemic challenges and timeliness issues
findings.detail: Recent Ofsted inspection identified areas of progress alongside continuing systemic challenges. Inspectors recognised improvements in leadership, partnership working and safeguarding practices, but areas requiring further improvement remain, particularly in relation to consistency of practice and timeliness of decision-making. The council has structured an improvement framework including an updated Children's Services Improvement Plan, strengthened corporate oversight, work with external advisers, and workforce recruitment focus, but acknowledges this requires sustained focus over time and remains a key area of corporate risk.
findings.matters: Systemic practice challenges and timeliness issues in children's social care represent both compliance risk and potential future cost exposure if outcomes worsen or legal challenge increases.
findings.figures: Recent Ofsted inspection (monitoring visits September 2024 – January 2025 and November 2025)
findings.quote: The most recent inspection identified areas of progress alongside continuing systemic challenges, consistent with the profile of a large and complex authority managing sustained service demand. Inspectors recognised improvements in leadership oversight, partnership working, and the strengthening of key safeguarding practices. However, areas requiring further improvement remain, particularly in relation to consistency of practice and the timeliness of decision making.

findings.headline: Internal audit identified limited assurance for particular services due to control weaknesses
findings.detail: The Head of Devon Assurance Partnership's 2025-26 opinion will report a mix of assurance levels. While overall Reasonable Assurance will be provided (reflecting positively on internal controls), Limited Assurance will be provided for particular services where audit work has demonstrated that more action is required in relation to key internal controls. The statement acknowledges this will become more challenging as Local Government Reorganisation implementation is known.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance opinions indicate material control weaknesses in specific service areas that require remediation, creating compliance and financial management risk.
findings.figures: Mix of assurance opinions with Limited Assurance in particular services
findings.quote: The assurance opinion due to be reported to the Audit Committee in June 2026 will summarise its work for 2025-26 and will give a mix of assurance opinions. Reasonable Assurance (which reflects positively on the internal controls in place) will be provided overall, with Limited Assurance provided for particular services where audit work has demonstrated that more action is required in relation to key internal controls.

findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit of £176.5 million with demand continuing to grow despite reform plan dependency
findings.detail: Devon has accumulated a DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) High Needs Block deficit of £176.5 million after DfE contributions and in-year surplus balances. Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) stand at 10,541 as of March 2026 with sustained growth in both volume and complexity. The council faces a complex challenge: the Government has shifted from Safety Valve agreements to requiring SEND Reform Plans, with potential write-off of up to 90% of accumulated deficits contingent on delivering credible, deliverable reform plans. However, this introduces new delivery and performance risk, and reforms will take time to deliver and depend on system-wide change across education, health and care partners.
findings.matters: A £176.5 million deficit is a material financial liability. The council's ability to resolve this depends on external partners and government approval of reform plans, creating significant financial and delivery risk for a lender to assess.
findings.figures: £176.5 million DSG deficit; 10,541 EHCPs as of March 2026; £9.4 million management actions delivered in 2024/25
findings.quote: the Council has accumulated a DSG deficit of £176.5 million, which is after contributions from the Department for Education and in-year surplus balances across the DSG. Demand for SEND support has continued to increase, both in volume and complexity of need, reflected in sustained growth in the number of Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), currently standing at 10,541 (March 2026).

findings.headline: Council faces continued DSG deficits through 2027/28 with government signalling support will become more limited
findings.detail: The DSG statutory override remains in place until end of 2027/28. The paper states: "For deficits that arise in 2026/27 and 2027/28, local authorities can expect that an appropriate and proportionate approach will continue, though it will not be unlimited." This signals the government recognises future deficits but will not fund them indefinitely, leaving councils to manage structural costs themselves from 2027/28 onwards.
findings.matters: This implies the council should expect further DSG deficits and must plan for material balance sheet impact in 2026/27 and 2027/28, with no certainty of future government support
findings.figures: Override ends 2027/28; future SEND funding model changes from 2028/29
findings.quote: For deficits that arise in 2026/27 and 2027/28, local authorities can expect that an appropriate and proportionate approach will continue, though it will not be unlimited.

findings.headline: Total EHCPs growing at 6.1% with average costs rising to £17,090, indicating demand outpacing budget containment
findings.detail: Total EHCPs increased from 9,937 in March 2025 to 10,541 in March 2026 (6.1% growth, slowing from 10% prior year). Simultaneously, average cost per EHCP rose from £16,886 to £17,090. While the number remains 99 below the Safety Valve forecast, the combination of volume and rising unit costs continues to pressure the budget.
findings.matters: Persistent demand growth combined with rising unit costs creates an unsustainable trajectory for the DSG and suggests underlying demographic or service pressures that structural changes have not yet arrested
findings.figures: 10,541 total EHCPs (vs 9,937 prior year); 6.1% growth; average cost £17,090 (up £204 from £16,886)
findings.quote: The total number of EHCPs as at March 2026 is 10,541 (vs 9,937 in March 2025)... average costs rising to £17,090 March 2026 (vs £16,886 in March 2025).

findings.headline: Independent special school placements have grown to 12.72% of EHCPs, far exceeding England average, driven by insufficient local capacity
findings.detail: Devon's reliance on independent special schools has increased significantly. As of January 2025, 9.10% of Devon learners were in independent schools versus the England average of 5.33%; by March 2026 this had increased to 12.72%. Placement numbers rose by 186 learners to 1,237 total. The paper explicitly states this is due to "insufficient local placements and reduced parental confidence in mainstream provision".
findings.matters: This indicates the council has not delivered its SEND provision strategy, forcing reliance on more expensive independent placements and creating structural cost growth that cannot be easily reversed
findings.figures: 12.72% in independent schools (March 2026); 1,237 placements (up 186); England average 5.33%
findings.quote: The current number of plans within Independent Special Schools has increased to 12.72%... Placement numbers have increased by 186 to 1,237 as at March 2026, driven by insufficient local authority school capacity and a lack of parental confidence in mainstream settings.

findings.headline: Safety Valve savings plan delivered only £10.7 million of £22.5 million (48%), with £9.1 million undelivered from provision creation programmes
findings.detail: Under the now-closed Safety Valve agreement, Devon identified £22.5 million in management actions but achieved only £10.7 million (48%). The £9.1 million undelivered savings relates to "Investing in Schools by Getting the Basics Right", indicating delays in creating additional special school and resource base capacity. This signals inability to manage demand through local provision.
findings.matters: Failed delivery of a major savings programme and inability to create sufficient local capacity shows structural budget management risk and dependency on government funding
findings.figures: £22.5 million target; £10.7 million achieved; £11.8 million undelivered (£9.1 million from Investing in Schools)
findings.quote: Of the £22.5 million management actions identified in the Safety Valve, £10.7 million has been achieved. £9.1m of the undelivered savings relate to the "Investing in Schools by Getting the Basics Right" programme.

findings.headline: In-year DSG overspend of £59.7 million, £15.6 million above forecast, driven by placement growth the council cannot control
findings.detail: The High Needs Block overspent by £59.7 million in 2025-26, representing a £15.6 million variance from the £44 million budgeted overspend. The primary driver was SEN Mainstream, which overspent by £10.8 million due to 606 Plus Packages exceeding budget, plus £4.6 million for tutoring 87 pupils over budget, and £4 million for 186 independent school placements over budget.
findings.matters: Significant and recurrent overspends indicate structural budget pressures and weak demand management, signalling ongoing fiscal strain
findings.figures: £59.7 million total overspend; £15.6 million net variance; £10.8 million SEN Mainstream overspend
findings.quote: Dedicated Schools Grant is reporting an overspend of £59.7 million which represents a net in-year overspend of £15.6 million over that budgeted (£44 million).

findings.headline: Council must fund £26.9 million of the DSG deficit from general reserves as High Needs Stability Grant is released in autumn 2026
findings.detail: The DSG cumulative deficit stands at £176.5 million. While the government is funding 90% of it (£191.3 million) through the High Needs Stability Grant, Devon must contribute the remaining 10% (£26.9 million) from its own resources. This represents a real drawdown on council balances.
findings.matters: This is a significant and imminent liability on the council's balance sheet that lenders will scrutinize when assessing available reserves and financial resilience
findings.figures: £26.9 million; £176.5 million cumulative deficit; £191.3 million government contribution
findings.quote: This is currently sat at £191.3 million and will be released to LAs in Autumn 2026... This means that the Authority will need to contribute to the balance of £26.9 million.

findings.headline: Council is operating under a SEND Safety Valve agreement with enhanced government monitoring.
findings.detail: Devon is submitting monitoring reports to government on a SEND Safety Valve agreement. Cabinet subsequently established an enhanced review process for how these monitoring reports are considered, following the Audit Committee's recommendation. Safety Valve agreements are government intervention schemes for councils with uncontrollable SEND cost pressures.
findings.matters: Safety Valve agreements indicate the council is in financial difficulty in this service area and has negotiated government tolerance of overspending.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: the Committee recommended that the relevant Cabinet Members for SEND, Finance, and the Leader of the Council were provided with copies of the Monitoring Reports the Council submits to Government on delivery of the SEND Safety Valve agreement.

findings.headline: Audit Committee requested reserves replenishment strategy, signalling reserves are being depleted.
findings.detail: In response to external auditor findings, the Committee requested that a reserves replenishment strategy be presented to them. This indicates reserves are being drawn down and the council needs to plan for rebuilding them.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion reduces the council's financial buffer and resilience to absorb spending pressures.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: requested a reserves replenishment strategy for the Council is presented to the Audit Committee.

findings.headline: Internal Audit gave Limited Assurance opinion on Children and Young People's Futures, indicating control weaknesses.
findings.detail: The Internal Audit End-of-Year Report gave an overall Reasonable Assurance opinion but a Limited Assurance opinion specifically in Children and Young People's Futures. This identifies control deficiencies or governance risks in a major service area.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance flags control or governance gaps that need remediation and could affect service delivery and financial management.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: Internal Audit's End-of-Year Report, including an overall opinion of Reasonable Assurance and a Limited Assurance opinion in Children and Young People's Futures.

findings.headline: Growing Dedicated Schools Grant deficit driving financial sustainability risks that Cabinet has escalated to government.
findings.detail: The Audit Committee identified concerns about a growing DSG deficit in relation to SEND. In response, the Cabinet Member for Children's Services escalated concerns to the Secretary of State for Education about cost apportionment between education and health and its impact on SEND delivery and the council's financial sustainability. Cabinet confirmed an enhanced review process was put in place following the Committee's recommendation.
findings.matters: DSG deficits represent uncontrollable cost growth in a statutory service area; escalation to government signals the council believes it cannot resolve this internally.
findings.figures: Not specified in the document
findings.quote: In early 2026, the Cabinet Member for Children's Services - SEND wrote to the Secretary of State for Education, copied to Devon MPs, highlighting cost apportionment between education and health and its impact on SEND delivery and the Council's financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: County Road Highway Maintenance Capital Budget 25-26, Proposals for 26-27 Programme and On-street Parking 26-27
findings.headline: Middle East instability creates emerging risk to material costs and supply chain availability for 2026/27 programme delivery.
findings.detail: The council identifies "ongoing instability in the Middle East" as a potential emerging risk "primarily through its influence on global supply chains, energy markets and material costs." The council states "Volatility in fuel prices and the availability of key construction materials is likely to continue" and has committed to "monitor impacts closely" but relies on "established relationships with contractors and suppliers" to mitigate. No contingency reserve or hedging strategy is described.
findings.matters: Material cost volatility directly affects capital programme delivery. A £100m budget with exposed commodity risk could see purchasing power shrink without contingency. The council's mitigation strategy appears passive (monitoring and contractor relationships) rather than active (reserves, contracts, procurement scheduling).
findings.figures: 2026/27 total capital budget £100.412 million exposed to material cost volatility
findings.quote: Ongoing instability in the Middle East presents a potential emerging risk to the delivery of the 2026/27 highway maintenance programme, primarily through its influence on global supply chains, energy markets and material costs. Volatility in fuel prices and the availability of key construction materials is likely to continue

findings.paper_title: County Road Highway Maintenance Capital Budget 25-26, Proposals for 26-27 Programme and On-street Parking 26-27
findings.headline: Severe weather in 2025/26—multiple named storms and record rainfall—forced repeated diversion of resources from planned maintenance programmes.
findings.detail: 2025/26 was marked by Storms Amy, Ingrid, and Chandra. Storm Chandra in January 2026 produced torrential rain and widespread flooding, cutting off communities, prompting multiple rescues, and "pushing the River Otter to its highest level ever recorded." The council reports that "resources repeatedly diverted to deal with severe weather conditions across the county," affecting planned programme delivery.
findings.matters: Increasing weather volatility creates unpredictability in asset maintenance costs and delivery. The council's planned programme depends on stable conditions; severe weather forces reactive spending and defers planned maintenance, worsening the backlog.
findings.figures: River Otter reached highest level ever recorded; funding diverted to emergency response
findings.quote: Chandra produced torrential rain and widespread flooding across Devon, particularly affecting, Exeter, Newton Poppleford, Otterton, Axminster and the A30 corridor, cutting off communities, prompting multiple rescues, and pushing the River Otter to its highest level ever recorded

findings.paper_title: County Road Highway Maintenance Capital Budget 25-26, Proposals for 26-27 Programme and On-street Parking 26-27
findings.headline: Government Local Government Reorganisation proposals have caused the council to avoid major procurement decisions and extend current highways contract to 2029 instead.
findings.detail: The council's term maintenance contract was extended to 31 March 2029 rather than undertaking a competitive procurement. The decision report states: "Cabinet recognised that the uncertainties arising from the Government's proposed Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) created significant risks for the County Council were any major procurement exercise to be undertaken at that time." This postponement freezes service delivery arrangements and supplier relationships for three years.
findings.matters: LGR uncertainty creates operational risk: the council cannot plan major service procurements, which may lock it into existing contract terms and prevent efficiency gains. Lenders need to understand whether the council has strategic control over service delivery and cost management.
findings.figures: Contract extension to 31 March 2029
findings.quote: Cabinet recognised that the uncertainties arising from the Government's proposed Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) created significant risks for the County Council were any major procurement exercise to be undertaken at that time.

findings.paper_title: County Road Highway Maintenance Capital Budget 25-26, Proposals for 26-27 Programme and On-street Parking 26-27
findings.headline: On-street Parking Account balance is reducing to just £79,000 by March 2027, eliminating buffer for income volatility.
findings.detail: The account is projected to reduce from £280,000 at March 2026 to £79,000 by March 2027. This account funds £3.368m in bus service subsidies, environmental improvements, and cycling. A balance of £79k provides virtually no buffer if parking income underperforms or unexpected costs arise. The account is now running at minimal prudential reserves.
findings.matters: A declining reserve with minimal closing balance signals tight cash management on this funding stream. If parking income drops or there is service disruption, the council has no buffer and would need to find alternative funding or cut bus subsidies (which serve 200 routes).
findings.figures: Projected balance March 2027: £79,000; bus subsidies from this account: £3.368 million (29% of all council bus subsidies)
findings.quote: The budgeted balance of the account is projected to reduce from £280,000 at 31 March 2026 to £79,000 by 31 March 2027.

findings.paper_title: County Road Highway Maintenance Capital Budget 25-26, Proposals for 26-27 Programme and On-street Parking 26-27
findings.headline: £11.6m of the approved 2026/27 highway budget is performance-based conditional funding that could be withheld if DfT compliance criteria are not met.
findings.detail: Of the 2026/27 DfT incentive fund, 50% is performance-based. The council's original budget included £23.3m as conditional, but DfT guidance clarified that only 50% of incentive funding can be conditional. This requires £11.6m to be reclassified from conditional to unconditional. If the council fails to meet undisclosed performance criteria, it could lose funding mid-year.
findings.matters: Budget certainty matters to lenders. A conditional funding arrangement means the council's approved budget could shrink during the year with no recovery mechanism. The council does not know the full performance criteria in advance.
findings.figures: £11,644,818 reclassified as conditional funding; £23.290 million total incentive fund (50% conditional)
findings.quote: the latest guidance from DfT has clarified that conditional funding is limited to 50% of the incentive fund. To reflect this, £11,644,818 needs to be moved from conditional to unconditional funding, per recommendation (b) of this report.

findings.paper_title: County Road Highway Maintenance Capital Budget 25-26, Proposals for 26-27 Programme and On-street Parking 26-27
findings.headline: Network condition deteriorated between 2024 and 2025 across all road classes, with principal A-roads showing deterioration for the first time.
findings.detail: 2025 SCANNER surveys show red condition proportions increased across all classes: A roads from 2.6% to 3.4%, B roads rose marginally, C roads from 13% to 15%, and unclassified roads remain at 24% in red condition. The council notes that A-road deterioration "suggests early signs of deterioration on principal routes." This is the first sustained deterioration on principal roads and represents a trend reversal.
findings.matters: Network condition trends matter to lenders because they signal whether the council is staying on top of its most critical assets. Deterioration on A-roads (strategic routes) is particularly concerning as these drive economic connectivity and generate the highest repair costs.
findings.figures: A roads: red increased from 2.6% to 3.4%; unclassified roads: 24% in red condition
findings.quote: A Roads: Red condition increased from 2.6% to 3.4%, with a corresponding rise in amber, suggesting early signs of deterioration on principal routes.

findings.paper_title: County Road Highway Maintenance Capital Budget 25-26, Proposals for 26-27 Programme and On-street Parking 26-27
findings.headline: Modelling shows a £390m backlog of repairs needed immediately, with £102m per year needed just to stop further decline.
findings.detail: In 2024 the council commissioned analysis which revealed two critical measures: a current backlog of £390m to repair all sections in red condition (needing maintenance within 12 months), and a steady-state annual requirement of £102m to maintain current condition over ten years. The council's total highway budget is £100m. The backlog reveals a structural funding deficit.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's assets are being maintained or deteriorating. A £390m backlog against a £100m annual budget shows the asset base is significantly underfunded and at risk of accelerating decline.
findings.figures: £390 million current backlog; £102 million per year steady-state requirement; 2026/27 approved budget £100.412 million
findings.quote: Current Backlog: £390 million. The backlog is the estimated cost to repair all sections in red condition, those needing maintenance within the next year, highlighting the scale of deterioration and the challenge of restoring the network to an acceptable standard.

findings.paper_title: County Road Highway Maintenance Capital Budget 25-26, Proposals for 26-27 Programme and On-street Parking 26-27
findings.headline: Devon has approved £15m additional borrowing for 2026/27 highway maintenance, plus a further £10m for the following four years.
findings.detail: On 24 February 2026, full Council approved the 2026/27 highway capital budget which included this additional capital investment. The council states this commitment enables a shift from "managing and mitigating decline" to "stabilising and strengthening" the network. This is material new borrowing driven by asset condition concerns and climate impacts.
findings.matters: New borrowing of this scale affects the council's total debt service, debt ratios, and future financial headroom. Lenders need to understand whether this is addressing a structural maintenance deficit or a cyclical gap.
findings.figures: £15 million for 2026/27; £10 million for following four years
findings.quote: In addition to the national DfT highways maintenance allocation, Devon County Council has committed a further £15 million of borrowing for highway maintenance in 2026/27.

findings.headline: On-street parking reserve depleted by £463,000, falling from £824,000 to £361,000 due to a shortfall against expenditure.
findings.detail: Parking income fell short of operating costs by £463,000 in 2025/26, eroding the reserve to a point where it may become insufficient to buffer future volatility. This is a minor issue in isolation but signals difficulty in cost recovery from this service.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves are a sign of underlying operational pressure; a lender would view shrinking reserves as reduced financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £824,000 opening balance; £463,000 deficit; £361,000 closing balance
findings.quote: The balance of the reserve has reduced from £824,000 to £361,000 at 31st March 2026

findings.headline: Corporate Services overspend of £1.4 million, with Legal Services demand pressure and income shortfall in SCOMIS.
findings.detail: Legal Services incurred £1.2 million overspend due to sustained high demand, despite vacancy management. SCOMIS (the council's property and asset management system) underachieved income by £1.5 million. These are internal service cost pressures that reduce financial headroom.
findings.matters: Sustained demand for legal services and underperformance in income-generating services suggest cost control challenges beyond frontline delivery; a lender would want to understand whether these are temporary or structural.
findings.figures: £1.4 million overspend; Legal Services £978,000 overspend; SCOMIS £1.5 million income underachievement
findings.quote: The outturn for Corporate Services shows an overall overspend of £1.4 million, after taking into account the carry forward of grants and contributions. Legal Services resulting in a £1.2 million overspend

findings.headline: Better Care Fund pooled budget with NHS is overspent by £2 million, shared equally between partners.
findings.detail: The £135 million integrated health and social care pool reported a 1.51% overspend, driven mainly by escalating costs in the Community Equipment Service and activity levels. The overspend is absorbed but signals cost pressures in joint commissioning arrangements and indicates the NHS partner also faces affordability challenges.
findings.matters: Overspend in integrated care arrangements suggests demand or cost control issues in health-social care interface; a lender would want to know whether the 50/50 risk share is sustainable or whether pressure will mount.
findings.figures: £2 million overspend (1.51% of £135 million pool)
findings.quote: the Better Care Fund (BCF), a pooled budget arrangement between the NHS Integrated Care Board and the Authority, totals £135 million for 2025/26 and is reporting an overspend position of £2 million (1.51%)

findings.headline: Children's independent placements overspend by £7.8 million due to increased reliance on costly external provision.
findings.detail: Despite a planned shift toward in-house residential capacity and increased foster care provision, the council saw higher demand than budgeted for independent residential children's homes. Recruitment targets for in-house foster carers were not met, forcing continued use of more expensive external placements. This is a live demand pressure, not a one-off variance.
findings.matters: Escalating placement costs in children's services are a national pressure. A lender would flag ongoing demand-driven overspend as a risk to medium-term budget stability, particularly given the £1 million additional spend on prevention.
findings.figures: £7.8 million overspend on independent placements; £1.2 million underspend on fostering due to unmet recruitment; £1 million targeted spending on children in need prevention
findings.quote: There is a £7.8 million overspend on independent placements, largely reflecting increased reliance on independent residential children's homes. Although the budget assumed growth in in-house foster care capacity, recruitment targets were not met

findings.headline: SEND deficit has accumulated to £176.5 million, growing by £50.8 million in 2025/26 alone.
findings.detail: Special Educational Needs provision is in structural deficit, with high needs costs continuing to outpace DSG funding. The government has announced support through the High Needs Stability Grant (90% of deficit) to be paid in autumn 2026, but this depends on Devon's SEND reform plan being approved by the DfE. The deficit sits outside the general fund but signals escalating demand for specialist provision.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this is a one-off DfE bailout or an ongoing liability that could revert to the general fund, and the effectiveness of the council's reform plan in controlling costs.
findings.figures: £176.5 million accumulated deficit; £50.8 million in-year increase; DfE grant expected £191.252 million (90% of £212.5 million owed)
findings.quote: The 2025/26 DSG SEND overspend transferred to the accumulated deficit is £50.8 million, increasing the accumulated deficit to £176.5 million

findings.headline: Budgeted savings shortfall of £3.8 million not achieved in full.
findings.detail: The council needed to deliver £21.7 million in savings but achieved only £17.9 million. Services identified alternative measures to partially mitigate the impact, allowing a breakeven position, but this reveals underlying challenges in savings delivery across multiple directorates.
findings.matters: Undelivered savings indicate budget management risk; a lender would want to understand whether this is cyclical or structural, and whether the authority can reliably hit efficiency targets.
findings.figures: £21.7 million budgeted delivery, £17.9 million achieved
findings.quote: savings of £17.9 million achieved against budgeted delivery of £21.7 million

findings.paper_title: DFP 26 62 Capital Monitoring (final outturn) 25.26 and Captial (Budget) 26.27
findings.headline: Zero capital receipts from asset disposals in 2025/26, against the estate's planned funding model.
findings.detail: The report states the estate normally generates capital receipts from asset sales, but the disposals table shows zero assets sold and zero capital receipts in 2025/26, with no planned disposals having completed by year end.
findings.matters: If the estate depends on capital receipts from asset sales to fund its capital programme, zero receipts indicates either disposal plans are delayed or the funding model is not delivering.
findings.figures: 0 capital receipts; 0 acres sold; 0 assets disposed in 2025/26
findings.quote: Most years the County Farms Estate generates significant capital receipts from the sale of surplus assets associated with an approved restructuring or rationalisation programme

findings.paper_title: DFP 26 62 Capital Monitoring (final outturn) 25.26 and Captial (Budget) 26.27
findings.headline: Capital programme underspend of £512,083 with £558,836 slippage from prior year.
findings.detail: The estate had £900,000 approved capital budget for 2025/26 plus £558,836 carried forward from 2024/25, totalling £1,458,836 available to spend. Actual spend was £946,753, resulting in £512,083 underspend to be carried forward to 2026/27.
findings.matters: Consistent capital underspend and slippage patterns signal potential issues with the council's ability to deliver capital programmes on schedule.
findings.figures: £512,083 underspend; £558,836 slippage from 2024/25; £946,753 actual spend
findings.quote: Total spend in 2025/26 amounted to £946,753 resulting in an underspend against the budget provision of £512,083

findings.headline: South West Norse management fees exceeded budget by £31,865 (11% overspend)
findings.detail: Fees for South West Norse (the managing contractor covering day-to-day estate management, maintenance procurement, and service contracts) came in at £331,865 against budget of £300,000, representing an 11% overspend with no explanation offered for the variance.
findings.matters: Unexplained contractor cost escalation reduces estate surplus and signals either poor cost control or scope creep in the management contract
findings.figures: Actual £331,865 vs budget £300,000 (overspend £31,865)
findings.quote: Actual spend for the South West Norse fees was £331,865 compared to the budget provision of £300,000.

findings.headline: Revenue surplus target missed for 2025/26, with the estate falling £11,198 short of £550,000 target
findings.detail: The estate delivered £538,802 against a target surplus of £550,000, representing an undershoot of 2%. While modest, this breaks a pattern described as consistent surplus delivery since 1992 and signals tightening margins.
findings.matters: The estate is a revenue-generator for the council's wider budget; even a 2% miss on a key funding source is material if the trend continues
findings.figures: Target £550,000; actual £538,802; overspend £11,198
findings.quote: The actual revenue surplus delivered by the Estate was £538,802 against the target surplus of £550,000. This effectively equates to an overspend of £11,198.

findings.headline: Quinquennial condition survey programme deferred from 2025/26 due to resource capacity issues
findings.detail: The routine structural condition survey of the farms was not delivered in 2025/26 and has been pushed out, attributed to 'resource capacity issues at a key time of the year.' This defers visibility of maintenance backlogs and emerging structural problems across the estate.
findings.matters: A planned condition survey programme kept deferred signals either weak asset management discipline or resource constraints, and leaves the council flying blind on accumulated maintenance risks
findings.figures: Budget £0 (programme not delivered)
findings.quote: The farms estate quinquennial condition survey programme was not delivered in 2025/26 due to resource capacity issues at a key time of the year.

findings.headline: Tenant Right Valuations overspent by £92,145 (185% of budget) due to disputed end-of-tenancy claims and unexpected dilapidation liabilities
findings.detail: Actual spend £142,145 against budget of £50,000. The overspend is attributed to 'end of tenancy valuations remaining in dispute at year end' and 'a significant contribution towards dilapidation remedial works on a number of farms where the repair liability changed from a landlords obligation to a new tenants obligation.' This suggests tenant disputes and emerging maintenance liabilities.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of contingent liabilities; disputed end-of-tenancy claims and mounting dilapidation work indicate the estate's liabilities may not be fully captured in budget forecasts
findings.figures: Actual £142,145 vs budget £50,000 (overspend £92,145)
findings.quote: This is partly due to a few end of tenancy valuations remaining in dispute at year end, and a significant contribution towards dilapidation remedial works on a number of farms where the repair liability changed from a landlords obligation to a new tenants obligation.

findings.headline: Rent arrears deteriorating rapidly, with arrears over 6 months nearly doubling in 3 months
findings.detail: Outstanding rent increased from £416,275 in February 2026 to £474,849 by end of May 2026 — an increase of £58,574 in just three months. Arrears over 6 months rose from £227,014 to £268,182. The report notes solicitors have been instructed to issue letters before action against some former tenants, indicating collection difficulties.
findings.matters: The estate's revenue surplus depends on rent collection; deteriorating arrears threaten the cash flow and the £538k surplus the estate provides to the wider council budget
findings.figures: Total arrears £474,849 (was £416,275); arrears over 6 months £268,181.64 (increase of £41,167.76)
findings.quote: A total of £416,275.01 was reported as outstanding at the February 2026 committee meeting... Tenants with rent arrears over 6 months 268,181.64 41,167.76

findings.headline: Partnership fee increases held below cost growth by offsetting through growth in external income
findings.detail: Partner day rate increases 3.0%, continuing a multi-year trend (2022/23–2025/26 range: 2.9% to 4.8%). The document explicitly notes this 'continues the trend of subsiding the Partner service delivery through generation of additional external income.' The budget assumes partner income of £2,058,459 and external income of £141,907. Sustainability depends on maintaining external contract growth.
findings.matters: If external income growth stalls or partners demand higher fee increases, the budget cannot be balanced without service cuts or council subsidy, creating a contingent liability for Devon.
findings.figures: Partner income £2,058,459; external income £141,907; partner day rate increase 3.0%.
findings.quote: This continues the trend of subsiding the Partner service delivery through generation of additional external income.

findings.headline: Employee costs rising 3.7% driven by ongoing pay increments from prior workforce changes, creating ongoing wage pressure
findings.detail: Staff costs increase from £1,989,843 to £2,062,990. The document attributes this to 'reshaping workforce profile in recent years [that] has led to more staff entitled to increments on top of the proposed 2026/27 pay award.' Prior years' recruitment and turnover created a cohort still accruing increments, producing ongoing wage cost growth independent of service growth.
findings.matters: Wage bill growth driven by prior staffing decisions rather than service need reduces future budget flexibility and makes balance harder to achieve if income growth falters.
findings.quote: Reshaping workforce profile in recent years has led to more staff entitled to increments on top of the proposed 2026/27 pay award.

findings.headline: Budget moved from requiring £54k cost cuts to balanced position entirely through income growth, with minimal contingency
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget required £54,087 of cost savings or additional income. The 2026/27 budget claims balance (Income/Savings Target £0.00) without requiring cost reductions. This is achieved by projecting income will grow by £114k (from £2,085,956 to £2,200,366), while costs are rising: employee costs +3.7%, only partially offset by reduced premises (-14.3%) and supplies (-7.6%). Reserves are £228,750, representing 10.4% of the £2.2m budget.
findings.matters: A budget that achieves balance purely through revenue growth with no financial buffer is fragile; any shortfall in partner demand or external income creates immediate pressure for council intervention, service cuts, or subsidy.
findings.quote: we have balanced budget that does not seek further savings or income generation, with the changes of recent years this is the most positive commencing position for some time due to more stability on income generation

findings.headline: Devon is experiencing severe winter weather requiring emergency Highways spending, with potholes 51% higher than the previous peak year.
findings.detail: Recent adverse weather (storms Goretti, Ingrid and Chandra) has caused significant damage to the road network. Reported potholes for January 2025 were 51% higher than January 2023/24 (the previous highest month on record). The council is spending an additional £3 million on reactive maintenance, gritting, and storm clear-up, including emergency works to protect coastal properties at Slapton, Torcross and Beesands.
findings.matters: While this appears to be weather-driven and potentially temporary, it reveals the council's vulnerability to climate/weather impacts as a rural authority responsible for extensive road and coastal infrastructure. Emergency spending is being funded from the SEND contribution release, which means it is displacing planned financial management. A repeated winter could force further borrowing or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £3 million additional Highways spend; potholes 51% higher than previous peak (January 2023/24)
findings.quote: The weather conditions over the winter period have caused a significant increase in Highways reactive works, impacting expenditure across numerous activities. For example, reported potholes for January 2025 were 51% higher than the same period in 2023/24, the previous highest period. Current projections indicate that an additional £3 million will be spent this year on repairing potholes, carrying out winter gritting and undertaking clear-up works following storms Goretti, Ingrid and Chandra.

findings.headline: Scomis (information systems service) is forecasting a £1.5 million deficit due to significantly reduced income forecast, with plans requiring reassessment.
findings.detail: Scomis is a shared information systems service. It is forecasting a £1.5 million deficit in 2025/26 primarily due to a significant change in expected revenue streams (external income). The report describes this as requiring 'a reassessment of operational plans and financial mitigation strategies,' suggesting the service model or external customer base has shifted unexpectedly.
findings.matters: An income-dependent service line suddenly losing significant revenue suggests either loss of external customers or a change in service demand that was not anticipated. This is a going concern risk for that service unit and indicates weak forecasting or market risk.
findings.figures: £1.5 million deficit forecast; described as result of 'significant change in expected revenue streams'
findings.quote: Transformation and Business Services are forecasting an overspend of £1.8 million, Scomis is now forecasting a deficit of £1.5 million, primarily due to a reduced income forecast. This shortfall reflects a significant change in expected revenue streams and will require a reassessment of operational plans and financial mitigation strategies.

findings.headline: The Better Care Fund (pooled budget with health) is forecasting a £2.2 million overspend, of which the council bears 50% responsibility—a shared risk it cannot control.
findings.detail: The Better Care Fund is a pooled budget between Devon County Council and Devon Integrated Care Board. The fund is forecasting a £2.2 million overspend, mainly from pressures in the Community Equipment Service. Under the pooling agreement, the council is responsible for 50% of any end-of-year deficit. The report indicates £1.1 million of this pressure is now reflected in the integrated adult social care forecast.
findings.matters: The council has accepted financial risk in a shared arrangement where it cannot unilaterally control spend. This is a structural governance issue: if the ICB's spending pressures continue, the council will face automatic liability without control over the underlying decision-making.
findings.figures: £2.2 million forecast overspend in Better Care Fund; £1.1 million reflected in integrated adult social care forecast; 50% council responsibility for any deficit
findings.quote: There continues to be a forecast overspend of £2.2 million associated with the BCF. This is mainly the result of pressures within the Community Equipment Service. Work continues to mitigate and reduce this risk, but the agreement that underpins the pooled budget arrangements mean that the Authority would be responsible for funding 50% of any end of year deficit.

findings.headline: Children's social care services are still in £1.7 million overspend, driven by external placements and agency staffing costs with no clear resolution.
findings.detail: Children and Young People's Futures services are forecasting a £1.7 million overspend (though improved from £3 million at Month 8). The position is primarily driven by external placements and staffing costs. While the council is improving agency staffing ratios, it continues to rely heavily on agency workers on the front line. Commissioning for children in care has a £2 million overspend due to placements in higher-cost settings than budgeted.
findings.matters: This is a structural service overspend driven by demographic and market forces (cost of placements, agency labour market), not temporary factors. The improvement from Month 8 to Month 10 is modest (£1.3 million reduction), suggesting the underlying cost drivers are not being controlled. This is likely to persist.
findings.figures: £1.7 million overspend in Children and Young People's Futures (improved from £3 million); £2 million overspend in Commissioning (placements); 812 children in care (down 10 from Month 8, but still above 832 budget)
findings.quote: Children's Social Care, following the budget transfer described in 3.12, is forecast to overspend by just under £2 million, an improvement of £1.5 million from month 8, this continues to primarily be driven by pressures within external placements and staffing.

findings.headline: The overall Month 10 underspend of £4.2 million is entirely dependent on releasing a £7.4 million SEND contribution that was previously planned, which is now uncertain due to DfE policy change.
findings.detail: The improved position reported at Month 10 (£4.2 million underspend vs £9.6 million worsening from Month 8) is driven by the release of a previously-budgeted £7.4 million contribution to SEND deficits. This release came only because the DfE changed its Safety Valve policy; the council had previously committed to this contribution. £3 million of this has been transferred to emergency Highways spending for winter storm damage. Without this one-off release, the council would be in overspend.
findings.matters: The reported financial improvement is not due to operational performance or genuine cost control, but a one-off policy change from central government. The underlying position is weaker than reported—without the SEND contribution release, the council would be overspending. This suggests reserves will be drawn more heavily than previously expected.
findings.figures: £7.4 million SEND contribution released; £3 million transferred to Highways; £4.2 million overall Month 10 underspend
findings.quote: Prior to this announcement the authority had agreed with the Department for Education and Treasury that the authority is not, and will not, be required to make contributions to the accumulated deficit as part of the Safety Valve agreement. The planned £7.4 million contribution to the SEND Deficit in 2025/26 is therefore no longer required and can instead be released to support the authority's overall financial position.

findings.headline: The council lost £10 million of Rural Services Delivery Grant funding this year with no replacement, a permanent structural reduction.
findings.detail: Devon lost its Rural Services Delivery Grant (which recognized the additional cost of providing services in rural areas) very late in the budget-setting process. A new Recovery Grant was introduced nationally but Devon received none of it. This is described as a structural loss that reduces the council's baseline funding permanently.
findings.matters: This is not a temporary saving but a permanent loss of revenue that must be absorbed or accommodated through service cuts or reserve drawdown. A large rural authority losing rural funding support while demand remains high is a significant structural pressure.
findings.figures: £10 million loss of Rural Services Delivery Grant; £0 received from new Recovery Grant
findings.quote: Devon is a large rural authority and has for many years received a Rural Services Delivery Grant that sought to recognise the additional cost of providing services in areas like ours. However, very late in the budget setting process last autumn, the new Government decided to repurpose that grant and we lost £10 million of much needed funding; a new grant, the Recovery Grant, was introduced but the authority received none of that new grant.

findings.headline: Budgeted savings of £21.7 million are tracking to deliver only £17.9 million, leaving a £3.8 million shortfall.
findings.detail: The council identified £21.7 million in planned savings but is now forecasting delivery of only £17.9 million. £4.7 million of planned savings are no longer considered deliverable, partially offset by £1.3 million of new plans or over-delivery. The report states 'work is ongoing' to address the shortfall, but provides no details of alternative mitigation.
findings.matters: A 17% shortfall in savings delivery indicates either unrealistic budget assumptions or weak implementation capability. This gap must be closed somewhere—either through additional service cuts, further reserve drawdown, or acceptance of deficit. It suggests the council's ability to manage its budget going forward may be constrained.
findings.figures: £21.7 million budgeted savings; £17.9 million forecast delivery; £3.8 million shortfall; £4.7 million identified as undeliverable
findings.quote: Budgeted savings of £21.7 million were identified as part of the budget setting process. At Month 8 Directorates are forecasting delivery of £17.9 million, giving a projected shortfall against the total target for the year of just over £3.8 million. This reflects £4.7 million of planned savings no longer considered deliverable

findings.headline: Accumulated SEND/DSG deficit has reached £180.1 million, £71.8 million worse than the council's Safety Valve agreement assumed.
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant is forecasting an overspend of £61.8 million in 2025/26 alone. The accumulated deficit has grown to £180.1 million by year-end, driven by rising numbers and costs of Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs). Average EHCP costs rose 5.6% in ten months (£16,886 to £17,832), and total EHCPs increased 4.4% to 10,360. This is excluded from the main budget position by statutory requirement but represents an enormous contingent liability.
findings.matters: This is a massive accumulated deficit on an accelerating trajectory. While the DfE has announced a grant covering 90% from autumn 2026, the council's responsibility for the remaining 10% (£27.2 million for 2025/26 alone, plus £15.3 million for 2026/27 and 2027/28) remains uncertain. The council had previously agreed NOT to contribute under its Safety Valve agreement; this changed only due to DfE policy shift.
findings.figures: £180.1 million accumulated deficit (£71.8 million above Safety Valve assumption); £61.8 million in-year overspend; 10,360 EHCPs at average cost £17,832; 4.4% year-on-year growth in EHCP numbers
findings.quote: Before any in year contributions from the DfE or the authority the DSG is forecasting an overspend of £61.8 million at Month 10... As at Month 10 the DSG cumulative deficit, net of reserves earmarked to support SEND, is forecast to be £180.1 million by the end of the year, £71.8 million more than the position included within the Safety Valve agreement

findings.headline: CSP growth is entirely council tax-driven, with government core funding contribution increasing only 0.3%
findings.detail: The council's narrative emphasizes a 14.1% CSP increase over the settlement period, but this figure includes the government's assumption of a 4.99% council tax rise. Removing council tax, actual core government funding grows just 0.3% in 2026/27. The authority explicitly states it will 'maximise this flexibility and increase the tax rate by 4.99%' to meet spending targets, creating exposure if collection rates fall short of the assumed 100% or if taxpayers resist further increases.
findings.matters: Lenders assess the sustainability of income sources; reliance on discretionary tax increases for core service funding is less resilient than grant funding, and has political/collection risk.
findings.figures: CSP increase 14.1% (with council tax); core funding increase 0.3% (without council tax); council tax increase assumed at 4.99%; assumed collection rate 100%
findings.quote: The increase in CSP of 14.1% is therefore entirely driven by the assumed council tax increases and not increased government funding.

findings.headline: Reserve transfer signals anticipated budget strain: £41.7 million moved from Resilience to Budget Management
findings.detail: The reserves strategy recommends transferring £41.7 million from the Resilience reserve to the Budget Management reserve to manage expected costs. This is made despite a stated strategy of 'living within our means' and no planned use of general balances to support the budget. The transfer suggests the council expects to draw down reserves to manage either undelivered savings or unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns indicate the council expects deficits or shortfalls; they erode the buffer available for genuine emergencies and raise refinancing risk if reserves fall below prudent levels.
findings.figures: £41.7 million transfer; minimum general balances recommended at £16 million
findings.quote: The reserves strategy includes a recommendation to transfer £41.7 million from the Resilience reserve to the Budget Management reserve.

findings.headline: SEND deficit spending of £73 million in 2026/27 with no end in sight despite government support announcement
findings.detail: The council spends £73 million more on high-needs SEND provision than the Dedicated Schools Grant covers in 2026/27 alone, described as 'expected to be just over £73 million and will only continue to increase in the medium term'. The High Needs Stability Grant (covering 90% of historic deficit) and two-year DSG Statutory Override extension to March 2028 provide partial relief, but the underlying demand-supply gap remains structural. The authority has transferred £41.7 million from its Resilience reserve to Budget Management reserve to manage this.
findings.matters: Persistent, growing overspend in a major service area (children's specialist education) indicates demand management failure; when government override ends in 2028, the council may face a choice between absorbing the cost or service cuts.
findings.figures: £73 million overspend in 2026/27; £41.7m reserve transfer; historic deficit grant covering 90%; DSG Statutory Override extends to March 2028
findings.quote: Spending in excess of grant in 2026/27 is expected to be just over £73 million and will only continue to increase in the medium term.

findings.headline: £39 million savings required in 2026/27 to achieve a balanced budget
findings.detail: The council states it cannot balance the 2026/27 budget from government settlement alone and must deliver £39 million in savings and alternative income. The budget notes this reflects inflation, national living wage (rising 4.1% to £12.71/hour), and demand pressures far exceeding the grant increase. The document acknowledges that 'delivery of the savings and the improvements in services through change programmes will not be easy' but expresses confidence based on 'rigorous budget process'.
findings.matters: Undelivered savings would create a budget shortfall; lenders assess the council's track record and capacity to execute £39m of changes without service disruption or reliance on reserves.
findings.figures: £39 million savings and new income required; inflation investment £29.9m; demand and priorities investment £42.2m
findings.quote: The Settlement is not enough for the Authority to set a balanced budget for 2026/27 without making budget savings and generating additional income, with inflation, national living wage together with demand for services driving cost increases well above the increase in available funding. Savings and new income of £39 million are reflected within service budgets to ensure services remain affordable.

findings.headline: Core government funding falls in real terms despite nominal CSP increase, with cuts accelerating from 2027/28
findings.detail: Excluding council tax, the council receives only £857,000 additional funding in 2026/27 (+0.3%), followed by £6.7 million reductions in both 2027/28 and 2028/29. Since inflation forecasts remain above 3%, this is a real-terms cut. The government's stated CSP increase of 14.1% over the settlement period is entirely dependent on assumed council tax rises and masks the withdrawal of real grant support.
findings.matters: Structural deterioration in sustainable funding creates dependency on discretionary council tax increases; lenders assess sustainability of income underpinning service delivery and debt repayment.
findings.figures: £857,000 (+0.3%) in 2026/27; -£6.7m (-2.3%) in 2027/28 and 2028/29; core funding increase of 0.3% places Devon 14th out of 21 county councils
findings.quote: Excluding Council Tax, the core funding increase is £857,000 (+0.3%). This is below inflation forecasts and therefore effectively a real terms cut in grant support, placing greater reliance on Council Tax to fund increasing costs and demand for local services.

findings.headline: SCOMIS audit abandoned mid-way; substantial change in future income context invalidated work
findings.detail: The Performance, Risk Management and Financial Sustainability of SCOMIS audit was concluded at draft stage without final opinion. The audit report notes: 'There was a substantial change in context linked to future income, this resulted in the work we had undertaken to date being rendered invalid and so the work was concluded at draft report stage.' No detail is provided on what the income change was or its scale.
findings.matters: An unfinished audit suggests a material shift in a system's financing was significant enough to make the audit framework obsolete; the nature and scale of this income change is material to council finances but undisclosed in this report
findings.figures: Unspecified change in future income context
findings.quote: There was a substantial change in context linked to future income, this resulted in the work we had undertaken to date being rendered invalid and so the work was concluded at draft report stage.

findings.headline: Trading Standards commercial income tracking absent; finance unable to access income forecasts or verify BDM value
findings.detail: Limited Assurance audit of Trading Standards' Business & Commercial Team found 'Finance has reported difficulties in accessing detailed income breakdowns and forecasts, often relying on historical data and finance system entries to estimate actuals for 2025/26.' More critically, 'There is no formal mechanism to monitor income directly attributable to the BDM role,' and 'The BDM has not delivered formal training sessions in their current role, despite expectations from Senior Management.'
findings.matters: Loss of income visibility and inability to attribute income to investment (BDM post) prevents proper accountability and raises questions about whether commercial spending is justified
findings.figures: No formal tracking mechanism for BDM-attributed income; finance relying on historical estimates
findings.quote: Finance has reported difficulties in accessing detailed income breakdowns and forecasts, often relying on historical data and finance system entries to estimate actuals for 2025/26... There is no formal mechanism to monitor income directly attributable to the BDM role.

findings.headline: Waste management risk escalated to high on corporate risk register; EPR payment uncertainty of £1.2m+
findings.detail: The corporate risk register recently escalated waste management to high risk due to potential overspend. The council estimated £1.2 million in Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) payments based on August 2024 data. The November 2025 Notice of Assessment was calculated by applying 1.93% to 2025/26 figures. The LAPCAP model is too complex for council to independently estimate, and PackUK may recalculate chargeable disposal costs as 'payments may fluctuate due to producer behaviour and regulatory changes.'
findings.matters: A high-risk waste budget with volatile, externally-calculated payments creates exposure to uncontrollable spending growth; the council cannot predict or constrain these costs
findings.figures: £1.2 million estimated EPR payment; 1.93% applied to 2025/26 figure; escalated to high risk on corporate register
findings.quote: The corporate risk register has recently escalated the waste management risk from medium to high, citing potential overspend... the November 2025 NoA letter states 'PackUK may recalculate chargeable disposal costs, and payments may fluctuate due to producer behaviour and regulatory changes.'

findings.headline: Alternative Education Provision audit found providers bypassed approval and placement agreements inconsistently stored
findings.detail: Limited Assurance rating for unregistered Alternative Education Provision identifies systematic application failures in interim commissioning process: 'Reviews of providers revealed missing documents, inconsistent HMRC verification, and evidence that newly onboarded providers had bypassed required senior management approval.' Individual Placement Agreements were 'inconsistently completed and stored,' and provider data returns 'declined significantly, limiting oversight.'
findings.matters: Unregistered providers with bypassed approvals and poor contract monitoring create risk of overspending on unsuitable provision and inability to verify value for money or provider quality
findings.figures: Multiple weaknesses identified across provider documentation; provider data returns declined significantly
findings.quote: Audit testing, however, found several weaknesses in the application of the interim process. Reviews of providers revealed missing documents, inconsistent HMRC verification, and evidence that newly onboarded providers had bypassed required senior management approval.

findings.headline: SEND provisions still lack end dates in system despite being upgraded from No Assurance; overpayment risk remains
findings.detail: The SEND audit was upgraded from No Assurance (June 2024) to Limited Assurance (September 2025), but significant data control problems persist. For historical provisions, only 9 of 40 older SOAP-approved placements had end dates recorded in the ONE system as of testing. For one budget code (8280-Personalised Budget), 79 of 189 cases still lacked end dates. While data migration is planned, this leaves the council unable to control spending on provisions that should have ended.
findings.matters: Without proper end dates on provisions, the council cannot control when SEND placements and associated payments should cease, creating direct overspend risk and potential waste of public funds
findings.figures: 79 out of 189 cases without end dates in one budget code; only 9 of 40 older provisions with recorded end dates
findings.quote: For one of the budget codes reviewed in 2024/25 (8280- Personalised Budget) there were still 79 out of 189 cases which did not have an End Date recorded on ONE when rechecked... Testing of (40) older provisions across three Senior Officer Approval Panels ( SOAP) dating from October 2024 to July 2025 showed that only nine of those 40 contained an End Date which was recorded on ONE.

findings.detail: Auditors plan to assess how internal controls in Children's Services have been strengthened, suggesting prior findings of control weaknesses from previous inspections (Ofsted/CQC) that remain being remediated.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses in high-value, high-risk service areas (especially those driving overspends) affect audit opinion risk and management integrity assessment.

findings.matters: Children's Services overspends are the fastest-growing pressure in English local government; active overspends signal demand not yet under control and budget risk.
