findings.detail: The new financial system is flagged as a specific area of focus for IT auditors during the current financial year. System implementations in their first year of operation carry control and data migration risks that could affect financial reporting reliability.
findings.matters: First-year ERP implementations can expose control weaknesses; auditors flagging it as a focus area suggests elevated risk around transaction processing and financial reporting accuracy.

findings.paper_title: Grant Thornton Audit Progress Report and Sector Update 2025 26 (Council and Pension Fund)
findings.headline: Devon is managing a Dedicated Schools Grant deficit through the national Safety Valve Programme
findings.detail: The audit will specifically assess how Devon has worked within the Safety Valve Programme to reduce its DSG deficit, including how the medium-term financial plan provision and demand reduction programs address this. The audit's focus on protecting cash position and increasing financial resilience points to this as a material concern.
findings.matters: DSG deficits directly consume council cash reserves and limit borrowing capacity; lenders track whether councils with Safety Valve obligations are on track to manage them.
findings.figures: No specific deficit figure given in this plan, but the focus on DSG deficit reduction and cash protection indicates material exposure.
findings.quote: assess the actions taken to reduce the annual DSG deficit in order to protect the cash position and increase financial resilience in the medium term. This includes how the council has worked within the Safety Valve Programme

findings.headline: Unprecedented funding settlement complexity creating budget-setting uncertainty
findings.detail: This is the first multi-year settlement in over a decade, consolidating 30+ separate funding streams into new grants, a complete business rates reset, and five new business rates multipliers. The paper notes 'the magnitude and complexity of the changes has led to a significant level of uncertainty when planning budget assumptions'. Clarity on allocations was only received 17 December 2025, and final settlement came 9 February 2026—weeks before council approval.
findings.matters: Complex funding structures and late settlement create planning risk. If allocations or formulas change, the budget could become unbalanced. The Fair Funding Review 2.0 reflects government determination to rebase funding, but transition periods are short and rules are still being written ('further details are expected to follow').
findings.figures: First multi-year settlement in 10+ years; 30+ funding streams consolidated; business rates reset from 1 April 2026; final settlement received 9 February, council approval 24 February
findings.quote: The magnitude and complexity of the changes has led to a significant level of uncertainty when planning budget assumptions, with clarity on local authority allocations only being received in the provisional settlement in late December.

findings.headline: Children's services receiving disproportionate budget growth (+7.7%) with continued demand and complexity pressures
findings.detail: Children and Young People's Futures services are budgeted for +7.7% growth (£19.1m increase), the largest uplift in the council. This reflects £19.9m in demand and growth pressures. Despite intervention through the Safety Valve programme and investment, demand continues to outpace allocations. The paper notes 'the continued growth in demand and complexity as well as a recognised adjustment within calculations'.
findings.matters: Children's social care is one of the largest drivers of council cost growth nationally. Even with above-average budget protection, demand is outpacing investment. This suggests the underlying drivers (demographics, complexity, safeguarding) are structural and unlikely to resolve through investment alone.
findings.figures: Children's services +7.7% budget increase (£19.1m); £19.9m growth pressures identified; £8.9m savings still required despite growth
findings.quote: The additional requirements to address the backlog of EHCPs, the continued growth in demand and complexity as well as a recognised adjustment within calculations has meant it has not been possible to contain Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) costs

findings.headline: Cost pressures of £72m (inflation, living wage, demand) only partially offset by budget growth of £33m
findings.detail: The budget includes £29.9m for inflation and National Living Wage, plus £42.2m for demand and other spending pressures, totalling £72m in gross growth requirements. Services receive only £33.2m (4.1%) growth from the base budget. The gap is closed by £39m in savings. This shows that even with significant savings, the council is still unable to fully fund cost growth.
findings.matters: Demand and cost growth significantly exceeds funding growth, forcing savings on top of investment. National Living Wage increases of 4.1% to 8.5% (depending on age band) are legislated, not controllable. Continued inflation above 3% erodes real purchasing power. This pattern will repeat in future years.
findings.figures: Inflation pressures: £15.6m; National Living Wage impacts: £14.3m; demand and other pressures: £42.2m; total growth: £72m; budget increase received: £33.2m (4.1%)
findings.quote: The Target Budgets for services reflect an estimated inflationary pressure of £14.3 million due to National Living Wage impacts... total investment of £29.9 million to cover inflation and national living wage plus £42.2 million to cover demand and other spending pressures

findings.headline: Reserve transfer of £41.7m from Resilience to Budget Management indicates contingency depletion
findings.detail: The reserves strategy includes a transfer of £41.7m from the Resilience reserve to the Budget Management reserve. General balances are being maintained at a minimum of £16m. This transfer of resilience funding to support the budget suggests the council is drawing down its contingency buffers to manage the structural gap between costs and funding.
findings.matters: Drawdown of resilience reserves to support the budget is a warning sign that funding shortfalls are not being met by efficiency alone. If this pattern continues, the council will face very limited buffers for unexpected costs or demand spikes. Minimum reserves strategies are reactive rather than proactive.
findings.figures: £41.7m transferred from Resilience reserve to Budget Management reserve; general balances minimum of £16m
findings.quote: The reserves strategy includes a recommendation to transfer £41.7 million from the Resilience reserve to the Budget Management reserve.

findings.headline: Business rates baseline cut by 15.3% in funding settlement due to reset
findings.detail: The April 2026 business rates reset, the first full overhaul in over a decade, reduced Devon's business rates baseline funding from £143.6m to £121.6m—a loss of £22m. The settlement includes new transitional arrangements to soften impact, but the reset reflects reallocation rather than protection. Five distinct rates will replace the current two, targeting small businesses, retail/hospitality/leisure, and high-value properties.
findings.matters: A £22m reduction in a relatively volatile funding stream increases exposure to economic downturn. Transitional arrangements are temporary, so the lower baseline persists. The shift to five multiplier rates could increase volatility if some property categories decline.
findings.figures: Business rates baseline: £143.6m (2025/26) → £121.6m (2026/27), a loss of £22m or -15.3%
findings.quote: Business Rates Baseline funding** 143,566 121,559 -15.3%

findings.headline: £39 million savings requirement embedded in service budgets with uneven impact across directorates
findings.detail: To balance the budget, Devon has identified £39m in savings, alternative funding and additional income. Children and Young People's Services must deliver only £8.9m of these despite a £19m growth requirement, receiving 7.7% budget growth. Public Health is cut 7.8% and Performance & Partnerships 8.1%. This creates unequal savings pressure and suggests decisions have been made to protect one service at the expense of others.
findings.matters: Large savings requirements raise delivery risk. Uneven distribution suggests protections for specific services (children's social care) at the expense of preventative services. Public Health reductions of 7.8% during a statutory public health duty period is material.
findings.figures: £39 million total savings and additional income required; Children's services saves only £8.9m despite £19.9m growth; Public Health cut by £1.2m (-7.8%); Performance & Partnerships cut by £0.5m (-8.1%)
findings.quote: Savings and new income of £39 million are reflected within service budgets to ensure services remain affordable.

findings.headline: Core funding declining in real terms: only +0.3% growth in 2026/27, then -2.3% for two years
findings.detail: Excluding council tax, Devon's core funding increases just £857k (+0.3%) in 2026/27, followed by cuts of £6.7m (-2.3%) in both 2027/28 and 2028/29. This represents a -4.3% decline since 2025. The paper explicitly states this is below inflation (still above 3%), meaning real-terms cuts. The only reason overall Core Spending Power looks positive (4.9%) is due to assumed council tax rises of 4.99%.
findings.matters: Real-terms funding cuts in future years, combined with structural cost pressures (inflation, National Living Wage), force additional savings or council tax rises. Devon ranks only 14th out of 21 county councils on core funding growth, limiting flexibility and raising questions about service sustainability.
findings.figures: Core funding +£857k (+0.3%) in 2026/27; -£6.7m (-2.3%) each of 2027/28 and 2028/29; overall -4.3% since 2025 excluding council tax; 3%+ inflation assumption
findings.quote: This is below inflation forecasts and therefore effectively a real terms cut in grant support, placing greater reliance on Council Tax to fund increasing costs and demand for local services.

findings.headline: £73m annual overspend on SEND budgets continuing despite intervention programme
findings.detail: Devon has been in the Department for Education's Safety Valve programme since March 2024, securing £95m between 2024-2032. Despite this, demand continues to outpace funding. For 2026/27, spending is expected to exceed government's grant funding by just over £73m. The safety valve programme will end 1 April 2026, replaced by a universal High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of historic deficits. However, accruing deficits for 2026-27 and 2027-28 require additional support whose terms have not yet been confirmed.
findings.matters: A £73m annual structural overspend on a statutory duty signals systemic underresourcing and carries intervention risk. The transition from Safety Valve to DSG Statutory Override (ending March 2028) creates uncertainty about future central support and whether councils will be forced to fund ongoing deficits from general revenue.
findings.figures: £73 million annual overspend in 2026/27; £95 million investment 2024-2032 under Safety Valve; 90% of high needs DSG deficit to be covered by new grant; DSG Statutory Override extends to March 2028
findings.quote: Despite ongoing support from the Department for Education and implementation of the authority's improvement plan demand for services continues to increase. Devon, along with other authorities, continues to see its spend significantly in excess of the government's grant funding. Spending in excess of grant in 2026/27 is expected to be just over £73 million

findings.headline: Highways maintenance programme disrupted by weather events, affecting ability to repair safety defects
findings.detail: Recent weather events have made it harder to repair highway safety defects quickly and sustainably. Routine planned maintenance is being disrupted, with regular maintenance programmes increasingly affected as a result.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance creates future capital backlogs and emergency spending. Safety defect accumulation also creates potential liability risk if repairs are chronically delayed.
findings.figures: Weather events disrupting highway maintenance capacity
findings.quote: About the condition of the highways network and related infrastructure, and the way recent weather events have made it harder to repair safety defects quickly and in a sustainable way. Members noted that this is disrupting routine, planned maintenance, with regular programmes increasingly affected as a result.

findings.headline: Library service savings assumed in 2026/27 budget before public consultation has ended
findings.detail: Savings for Library and Information Services are assumed in the draft budget, but the final budget is being presented before consultation has concluded and with implementation timelines still fluid. This creates risk that consultation findings may require reversal or reduction of the savings.
findings.matters: Assumed savings not yet confirmed through consultation process are budget delivery risk. Political or operational pushback could force removal of the savings from the plan.
findings.figures: Library savings assumed before consultation end
findings.quote: That savings are assumed for Library and Information Services within the draft 2026/27 Budget. Members noted that the final draft budget is due to be presented to Cabinet and Council before the public consultation has concluded, and at a time when the proposed implementation timeline remains fluid.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care transformation savings dependent on NHS partnership facing its own budget cuts and reforms
findings.detail: Integrated Adult Social Care transformation savings are heavily dependent on successful NHS partnership working, but the NHS is itself affected by ongoing reforms and significant budget reductions. The budget risk assessment flags both financial and operational risks from this dependency.
findings.matters: If the NHS cannot deliver on shared transformation outcomes due to its budget constraints, the council faces the risk that assumed savings will not materialise, creating a budget deficit.
findings.figures: NHS experiencing significant budget reductions
findings.quote: That the delivery of Integrated Adult Social Care transformation savings is heavily dependent on successful partnership working with the NHS, which is itself affected by ongoing NHS reforms and significant reductions to its budget, and that this dependency poses both financial and operational risks to the Council as outlined in the budget risk assessment.

findings.headline: Public Health Grant at £39 per head is significantly below national average, with uncertain future burdens
findings.detail: Devon's central Government grant allocation to Public Health remains among the lowest in the country at £39 per head, with ongoing uncertainty around future Public Health burdens that may place additional pressure on the grant.
findings.matters: Low public health funding relative to need forces either service reductions or absorption of costs from reserves. Future burden uncertainties make medium-term planning difficult.
findings.figures: £39 per head – among lowest in country
findings.quote: That the central Government grant allocation to Public Health in Devon remains among the lowest in the country, at £39 per head, and that the ongoing uncertainty around future Public Health burdens may place additional pressure on the Public Health Grant and affect the Council's ability to plan effectively.

findings.headline: Devon schools are relatively under-funded compared to national formula, affecting SEND provision investment
findings.detail: The f40 group highlights Devon's relative underfunding in schools finance. This limits the council's ability to invest in school estates to meet SEND demand, putting pressure on the council to fill gaps.
findings.matters: Underfunding of statutory services like SEND education creates pressure on the council's own budget if it must make additional investment or meet statutory duties schools cannot afford.
findings.figures: Devon identified by f40 group as relatively underfunded
findings.quote: Devon's continuing relative underfunding in schools finance (as highlighted by the f40 group), and the associated pressures this places on schools. Furthermore, the impact this has on the ability to adapt and invest in school estates required to meet the needs of children and young people with SEND to be educated in inclusive mainstream education.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant pressures escalating in High Needs Block with unclear future funding reforms
findings.detail: Scrutiny notes continuing pressure and uncertainty surrounding the Dedicated Schools Grant, particularly the High Needs Block, with awaited clarity on future funding reforms from Government that remain unconfirmed.
findings.matters: DSG pressure, especially High Needs, creates forward-looking revenue budget risk. These deficits have accumulated across many English councils and represent a structural sustainability issue.
findings.figures: High Needs Block within Dedicated Schools Grant under pressure
findings.quote: The continuing pressure and uncertainty surrounding the Dedicated Schools Grant, particularly within the High Needs Block, the associated risks to the Council and awaited clarity on future funding reforms from Government.

findings.headline: Local Government Finance Settlement remains unfinalised, creating budget preparation uncertainty
findings.detail: Scrutiny recorded concern that the final settlement had not been provided, which poses risks for budget preparation and the council's ability to develop a robust budget. The council is preparing its budget without confirmation of its income settlement.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the budget is built on confirmed, not provisional, funding allocations. Late settlement changes can create gaps between assumed and actual income.
findings.figures: Final settlement not provided at budget-setting stage
findings.quote: That the final Local Government Finance Settlement had not been provided. This uncertainty poses risks for budget preparation, financial planning, and the Council's ability to develop a robust budget for the forthcoming year.

findings.headline: Business Rates base at risk from business failures; council monitoring April 2026 Business Rates changes
findings.detail: The council notes that "business failures will impact the Business Rates base" and is "closely monitoring impacts related to changes in Business Rates from April 2026." The document provides no detail on what those changes are or the scale of risk, but flags it as a live concern. Combined with lower-than-average wages in much of Devon and high cost-of-living pressures, this suggests a material risk to non-domestic revenue forecasts.
findings.matters: Business Rates are a material non-controllable income stream for local authorities. A lender would want to understand the scale of the April 2026 changes and whether Devon has modelled the impact on its base.
findings.figures: £679.80 average full-time earnings in Devon (vs £766.60 UK average); below-average incomes across much of the county; multiple deprivation hotspots in Ilfracombe, Exeter, Barnstaple
findings.quote: The continuing high cost-of-living is likely to increase the number of residents who need help with Council Tax payments, whilst business failures will impact the Business Rates base, with the Council closely monitoring impacts related to changes in Business Rates from April 2026

findings.headline: Household Support Fund reduced and replaced with new fund, ending free school meal vouchers
findings.detail: The government's Household Support Fund, which Devon administers to residents, is being cut from £8.9m (2025/26) to an estimated £8.4m under a new Crisis and Resilience Fund (from April 2026). The council notes this change will bring "significant changes in how residents can access support," and "The delivery of free school meal vouchers to families in holidays is likely to end within these new arrangements." This loss of both funding and a policy tool to support vulnerable households could increase pressure on council tax collection and place-based need assessments.
findings.matters: A lender would track reductions in the council's ability to manage demand-side pressures (poverty relief) and any risk that loss of external funding translates into pressure on the council's own finances or collection rates.
findings.figures: £8.9 million Household Support Fund (2025/26); £8.4 million estimated Crisis and Resilience Fund allocation (2026/27 onwards); £5.725 million to £28.567 million additional council tax revenue depending on precept increase chosen
findings.quote: The Government have reduced Devon's HSF funding in 2025/26 to £8.9 million resulting in a reduction primarily in crisis funding for residents. The Government have announced that the Household Support Fund will be replaced by a new Crisis and Resilience Fund from April 2026. Devon's allocation is likely to be £8.4 million. The impact and delivery of this fund will see significant changes in how residents can access support

findings.headline: Children's Social Care demand cost pressures rising faster than savings targets can accommodate
findings.detail: Children's Social Care budget has risen 10.1% (£18.3m) to £199m, driven by placement demand growth: fewer foster carers means more children placed in residential homes, which cost significantly more. The council has allocated £7.8m to meet current demand pressures but plans to save only £6.9m across all initiatives (placement sufficiency, workforce retention, service reviews). The cost of residential places is explicitly stated as increasing, and complexity of need is rising, creating a structural gap between growing costs and the savings the council can realise.
findings.matters: This is a service-specific demand spiral: costs are driven by demography and market prices (residential placement fees), not controllable by the council, while savings come from discretionary programmes (workforce stability, placement sufficiency). If demand growth outpaces the savings, the shortfall will recur in future years.
findings.figures: £199 million Children's Social Care budget (10.1% increase); £7.8 million growth allocation for placements; £6.9 million planned savings; £3.2 million for foster carers; £4.5 million for residential sufficiency; £2.2 million for social worker recruitment
findings.quote: In common with its regional neighbours, Devon is experiencing increased costs to provide homes and support for children and young people who need them. A reduction of foster carers over time and increased complexity of need means that more children and young people are being placed in a children's home setting. The costs of these types of homes is also increasing

findings.headline: Adult Social Care £21.1m savings plan depends entirely on a transformation programme that has not yet delivered
findings.detail: Devon's adult social care budget of £395.9m requires £21.1m in savings and income initiatives to balance, alongside £15.8m in National Living Wage pressures. The council is partnering with Newton to deliver a 'Living Well in Devon' transformation programme, which will supply "skills transfer and co-designing solutions." The budget document explicitly states that achieving these savings is dependent on "the directorate being able to give focus to the timely and successful delivery" of this programme. If the transformation underperforms, the budget will not balance.
findings.matters: The council has a material budget gap in its largest service area that is contingent on a discretionary transformation programme. If execution fails or slips, there is no identified fallback and the council would face a mid-year shortfall in a service that is growing due to National Living Wage pressures.
findings.figures: £395.9 million Integrated Adult Social Care budget; £21.1 million in planned savings and alternative funding; £13.7 million of inflation from National Living Wage alone; NLW rising from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour (4.1% increase)
findings.quote: Ultimately, achieving these savings, and the positive impacts for our residents and staff will be dependent on the directorate being able to give focus to the timely and successful delivery of the Living Well in Devon Programme

findings.headline: SEND funding will not achieve full sustainability despite £95m Safety Valve investment
findings.detail: Devon has secured £95m from the DfE Safety Valve programme (2024–2032) to address SEND cost pressures, but the council states this will not deliver full sustainability in the medium term. The council has transferred £73.3m to a ring-fenced adjustment account to manage the gap. The government's SEND White Paper, expected early 2026, will introduce significant changes with unknown financial implications that may require a budget refresh.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about a committed, material cost pressure (SEND) that the council explicitly identifies as structurally unfunded and dependent on forthcoming policy changes beyond its control.
findings.figures: £95 million Safety Valve investment (2024–2032); £73.3 million transferred to ring-fenced adjustment account; High Needs Block £134.4 million (before deductions); 5.9% of Devon pupils have EHCPs (above national average)
findings.quote: Current evidence indicates that additional DSG funding through the Safety Valve Agreement will not achieve full sustainability in the medium term. To mitigate this risk, £73.3 million has been transferred to a ring-fenced adjustment account

findings.committee: Corporate Infrastructure and Regulatory Services Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Capital financing costs rise to £39.646 million in 2026/27 (5.33% of revenue budget) from expansion of external borrowing
findings.detail: The shift to external borrowing increases revenue budget pressure. Capital financing costs in 2026/27 are projected at £39.646 million (comprising £14.662 million minimum revenue provision and £27.507 million interest payable), equivalent to 5.33% of the net revenue stream. This ratio is forecast to rise further to 5.40% in 2027/28 as additional borrowing is taken on, before declining in later years as debt repayment accelerates.
findings.matters: Higher financing costs permanently reduce resources available for frontline services. The upward trajectory in the first two years reflects the revenue impact of increasing debt levels, constraining the council's service delivery capacity during a period of other budget pressures.
findings.figures: £39.646 million capital financing costs 2026/27; 5.33% ratio to revenue stream; 5.40% in 2027/28; £27.507 million interest payable
findings.quote: The additional borrowing will incur additional capital financing costs to the revenue budget.

findings.committee: Corporate Infrastructure and Regulatory Services Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: £125.62 million of debt matures in 2026/27; refinancing strategy dependent on interest rates falling as forecast
findings.detail: The council has £125.62 million of external debt maturing in 2026/27 (£91.79 million short-term borrowing plus £33.83 million long-term loans), representing just under 20% of current external debt. Current strategy is to refinance initially on a short-term basis at approximately 4.5% per annum, with the intention of converting to longer-term fixed-rate debt when PWLB rates have reduced. This strategy assumes Bank of England base rate cuts and PWLB rate reductions during 2026.
findings.matters: Refinancing risk is material. If interest rates do not fall as anticipated, the council faces either locking into higher long-term rates (increasing financing costs) or maintaining a high proportion of short-term debt that requires frequent refinancing, creating ongoing market access risk.
findings.figures: £125.62 million maturing debt; 4.5% target refinancing rate; approximately 20% of total external debt; current external debt £529.84 million
findings.quote: Following the short term refinancing of £46.5 million of long term loans in 2023, and new borrowing undertaken on a short term basis, just under 20% of the Council's current external debt will need refinancing during 2026/27.

findings.committee: Corporate Infrastructure and Regulatory Services Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disability) deficit is the primary cause of cash depletion; government funding solution still awaited
findings.detail: The council's cash reserves have declined significantly because expenditure on SEND education provision exceeds government grant funding, with the deficit charged to an unusable reserve. This is explicitly identified as "the most significant reason" for cash depletion and the move to external borrowing. The council notes it is "still awaiting announcements from Government" on how to resolve SEND deficits. Without government intervention, this structural pressure will persist.
findings.matters: The SEND deficit is a statutory obligation that cannot be underfunded by law. If government does not provide additional funding, the council faces ongoing cash drainage, rising external debt, and increasing revenue pressure. This is the root cause of the borrowing requirement, not a capital spending choice.
findings.figures: SEND deficit amount not disclosed; charged to unusable reserve
findings.quote: At the time of writing this report, we are still awaiting announcements from Government on how they propose to resolve the deficits on SEND that are being experienced by local authorities across the country.

findings.committee: Corporate Infrastructure and Regulatory Services Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council transitions to external borrowing: £163.48 million required for 2026/27 as internal cash resources depleted
findings.detail: After years of containing capital expenditure through internal borrowing, Devon can no longer fund capital spending and debt refinancing from cash reserves. The 2026/27 strategy requires £163.48 million of external borrowing comprising £11.36 million for the capital program, £125.62 million to refinance maturing debt, and £26.50 million to refinance past internal borrowing. This reflects a fundamental shift in the council's financing model.
findings.matters: This marks a material increase in leverage, debt service costs, and dependence on market access. For lenders assessing the council's credit position, it signals that cash reserves—a key liquidity buffer—are now insufficient for operations.
findings.figures: £163.48 million external borrowing requirement; £553.13 million external debt as at 31 March 2026; forecast £590.99 million by year-end 2026/27
findings.quote: The reduced level of cash balances has meant that it is no longer affordable to fund capital expenditure from internal borrowing. Therefore, the £11.4 million of borrowing required for the 2026/27 Capital Programme will need to be met through external borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Devon County Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Bank account closures were not formally approved by Section 151 Officer in accordance with financial regulations
findings.detail: Fourteen nil bank accounts (7 with Barclays, 7 with Santander) were closed during the year without proper authorization. Council Financial Regulations require Section 151 Officer (CFO) approval for all account closures. For 14 identified closures, no evidence of CFO approval was provided, though Head of Financial Systems provided email approval for Barclays closures.
findings.matters: Failure to follow established financial regulations for bank account controls, even for nil-balance accounts, indicates governance control weaknesses and non-compliance with internal procedures.
findings.figures: 14 bank account closures without documented CFO approval; 7 Barclays, 7 Santander
findings.quote: For the 14 closures identified, no evidence of approval or delegated action from the Section 151 Officer was provided.

findings.paper_title: Devon County Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Pension liability of £132m is sensitive to small changes in discount rate and inflation rate assumptions
findings.detail: The council's net defined benefit pension liability stands at £132m as at 31 March 2025 (down from £145m prior year). A 0.1% change in discount or inflation rate assumptions would have approximately 1.5% effect on the liability (roughly £2m impact). Auditors identified this as a significant risk due to assumption sensitivity.
findings.matters: A £132m pension liability with high sensitivity to actuarial assumptions represents a significant financial commitment and balance sheet risk for lenders assessing financial position.
findings.figures: £132m net pension liability; £13m net actuarial gain in 2024/25; 0.1% rate change = 1.5% liability impact
findings.quote: A small change in the key assumptions (discount rate, inflation rate, salary increase and life expectancy) can have a significant impact on the estimated IAS 19 liability. In particular the discount and inflation rates, where our consulting actuary has indicated that a 0.1% change in these two assumptions would have approximately 1.5% effect on the liability.

findings.paper_title: Devon County Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Significant audit delays and quality issues in evidence gathering extending beyond planned timeline
findings.detail: The audit took significantly longer than anticipated to complete. Delays resulted from late receipt of evidence, insufficient evidence quality in some cases, poor responsiveness from service units (requiring multiple follow-ups), delays from the council's valuers, and errors in banker confirmations requiring corrected letters.
findings.matters: Extended audit timelines and quality issues in evidence gathering raise concerns about the council's financial reporting processes and internal controls environment.
findings.figures: Two banker confirmation errors identified and corrected; final audit fee increased subject to PSAA approval
findings.quote: The audit did, however, take significantly longer to complete than anticipated, due to delays in receiving evidence to support our testing and in responding to queries. We also noted that the quality of evidence was not sufficient to conclude testing in some cases.

findings.paper_title: Devon County Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: IFRS 16 implementation caused £10m reduction to PFI liability due to lack of coordination with partner authorities
findings.detail: The council identified differing approaches among three local authorities jointly holding an energy-from-waste PFI contract. After discussions, the Authority reduced its PFI liability by £10m after determining the IFRS 16 adjustment was incorrect. It had incorrectly reflected indexation on gate fees rather than capital elements only. Lack of joined-up approach delayed audit completion and required technical review.
findings.matters: A £10m balance sheet adjustment resulting from implementation coordination issues indicates governance and accounting process weaknesses.
findings.figures: £10m reduction to PFI liability; £10m transfer to revaluation reserve for Plymouth energy from waste plant
findings.quote: We identified differences in approach for the Plymouth energy from waste plant PFI between the three local authority partners. The Authority has adjusted its accounts, following discussions with its partner authorities.

findings.paper_title: Devon County Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Journal authorisation process over £200k remains a significant control weakness bypassed via email approval
findings.detail: The council's manual journal authorisation process for amounts over £200k is not automated and can be bypassed. Head Accountant email approval is required before processing but lacks system enforcement. Auditors assigned higher risk to these journals and undertook additional testing. The Finest system replacement (April 2025) is expected to introduce better automated controls.
findings.matters: Manual journal controls without system enforcement create material misstatement risk in financial statements and represent a recurring audit weakness.
findings.figures: Journals above £200k threshold; manual email-based control process for dataset journals
findings.quote: This is via e-mail, rather than an automated function within the system which means that the authorisation process could be bypassed.

findings.paper_title: Devon County Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Segregation of duties control weakness in new HeyCentric financial system with four users holding conflicting access
findings.detail: Four users with administrative access to HeyCentric also have financial responsibilities, creating a segregation of duties conflict. This allows individuals to bypass system-enforced internal controls, potentially enabling unauthorised system changes, account creation, privilege updates, or deletion of audit logs. Enhanced access was granted during implementation without review.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses in financial systems directly threaten the integrity of financial reporting and fraud prevention, impacting reliability of financial statements lenders depend on.
findings.figures: 4 users identified with conflicting administrative and financial access; system implemented 2024/25 without adequate segregation controls
findings.quote: Administrative access to HeyCentric has been granted to 4 users who have financial responsibilities. The combination of financial responsibilities with the ability to administer end-user security is considered a segregation of duties conflict.

findings.paper_title: Devon County Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Value for Money audit identified significant weaknesses across the council's arrangements
findings.detail: The auditors concluded they are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness. Significant weaknesses were identified relating to Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit, change programme effectiveness, and social care cost pressures with three key recommendations made in each area.
findings.matters: A finding of significant weaknesses in value for money arrangements indicates governance and financial management concerns that directly affect the council's ability to deliver services and manage resources sustainably.
findings.figures: £132m pension liability; £680m land and buildings; DSG deficit noted as significant concern
findings.quote: We identified significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Update Report For 2025-2026 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: Unit 4 finance system implementation diverting resources; prior-year audit observations remain unimplemented
findings.detail: The 2024-25 Key Financial Systems audit noted that many staff resources were devoted to the Future Finance Project (Unit 4 implementation). A number of prior-year audit observations remain where management plans have not been fully implemented, largely due to resources focused on the finance system transition. The council expects several outstanding items to be mitigated by the transition to Unit 4. Full audits of key financial systems will be undertaken in 2025-26 based on the new system.
findings.matters: Major system transitions create control risk if legacy control weaknesses are not cleared before cutover; unresolved prior-year observations during a system change period suggests the council may be running with weakened controls during a critical window.
findings.figures: Future Finance Project diverted resources during 2024-25; prior observations remain unimplemented
findings.quote: There remain a number of prior observations where management plans have not been fully implemented, largely due to resources focussed on the Future Finance Project, however, it is expected that several of those outstanding will be mitigated by the transition to Unit 4.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Update Report For 2025-2026 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: Capital projects database (PPlan) built on unsupported Microsoft Access platform with administrator gaps and business continuity risk
findings.detail: Audit of the Engineer Design Group's capital programme project management found that PPlan—the database system used to track capital projects—is built on Microsoft Access, which is not supported by Devon's ICT department. There is currently a lack of system administrators and administrator documentation, creating business continuity risk if the system fails. The audit supports the service's plan to transition to a new web-based system at the earliest opportunity.
findings.matters: Reliance on unsupported, poorly documented legacy systems for capital programme tracking creates continuity risk; project management data loss or system failure could impact the council's ability to track and report capital schemes to lenders or regulators.
findings.figures: System built on Microsoft Access (unsupported by ICT); no documented administrator procedures
findings.quote: There is currently a lack of system administrators and administrator documentation for PPlan, which poses a risk to business continuity should the system experience issues. Furthermore, Microsoft Access, the platform on which PPlan is built, is not supported by Devon's ICT department.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Update Report For 2025-2026 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: Subject Access Requests only achieving 42% compliance with 3-month statutory deadline
findings.detail: Audit of Freedom of Information and Subject Access Request (SAR) handling found a robust system for FOI, but SARs—which are often more complex and time-consuming—are only achieving around 42% completion within the statutory 3-month deadline. The Freedom of Information policy has not been reviewed since 2012 and is overdue for update.
findings.matters: Chronic failure to meet statutory data protection deadlines creates legal risk (ICO enforcement) and suggests resource or process constraints; outdated policy indicates lack of governance refresh.
findings.figures: 42% of SARs completed within statutory 3-month deadline (required: 100%); FOI policy last reviewed 2012
findings.quote: Subject Access Requests, which are often more complex and time-consuming, are only achieving around 42% completion within the statutory deadlines of three months.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Update Report For 2025-2026 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: Procurement card spend in schools rated Limited Assurance; VAT recovery gaps and policy breaches identified
findings.detail: Audit of procurement card spend across 111 schools (£750,455.73 spent in 2023-24) returned Limited Assurance. Testing of 585 transactions found 11 without receipt support. Missed opportunities to recover £818 in VAT due to lack of supporting receipts. Evidence found of staff using loyalty cards in breach of policy. Gaps identified in authorization evidence and confirmation that expenditure was made by the named cardholder.
findings.matters: Limited assurance on procurement controls indicates weaknesses in financial authorization and compliance; VAT recovery gaps represent lost income; policy breaches suggest insufficient oversight and training.
findings.figures: 111 schools; £750,455.73 spend in 2023-24; 11 of 585 transactions (1.9%) without receipts; £818 missed VAT recovery
findings.quote: There were missed opportunities to recover £818 in VAT where supporting VAT receipts had not been obtained. Testing also identified that there was evidence of loyalty cards being used by staff when making school purchases which is in breach of policy.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Update Report For 2025-2026 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: High unallocated funds sitting in Virtual Wallet managed account with no planned retrieval
findings.detail: The audit of the Virtual Wallet implementation (successor to Devon Card) found that as of April 2025, £1,166,278 was held in the Virtual Wallet, of which £248,985.94 sat in the council's managed account as unallocated funds. Audit flagged this level as high and noted no retrieval of surplus balances had been undertaken; there has been no recovery to allow for contingency during the Unit 4 system rollout.
findings.matters: Large unallocated balances tied up in a system suggest either overfunding or poor cash management; lack of clarity on why funds remain unspent raises questions about service delivery, planning accuracy, or financial control.
findings.figures: £1,166,278 total in Virtual Wallet; £248,985.94 unallocated in council managed account (as of April 2025)
findings.quote: As of April 2025, there was a balance of £1,166,278.00 in the Virtual Wallet, £248,985.94 of which was sat in Devon County Councils' managed account in Virtual Wallet (unallocated funds). This level is considered high, however, it is acknowledged that there has not been any retrieval of surplus balances undertaken to allow for a contingency in the event of any issues with the roll out of the Council's new finance system, Unit 4.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Update Report For 2025-2026 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: Ofsted complaint handling process failing to meet 28-day statutory deadline, with 37.5% of cases late
findings.detail: Audit of the council's Ofsted-referred school complaints process found systemic timeliness failures. Of 120 complaints logged during 2024-25 academic year (to July 2025), 84 were closed with 32 (38%) exceeding the 28-school-day deadline. Of 36 open cases, 13 are already overdue. Overall 37.5% of all complaints were or will be late. The documented process is outdated, referencing legacy structures and staff no longer in post.
findings.matters: Failure to handle statutory complaints within required timelines creates legal exposure and suggests weak process control; in social services-adjacent work, timeliness failures can indicate broader governance or capacity issues.
findings.figures: 120 complaints logged; 84 closed with 32 (38%) over deadline; 36 open with 13 overdue; 37.5% total late rate; 28-day deadline required
findings.quote: Of these, 84 (70%) were closed and 36 (30%) remained open. Among the closed cases, 32 (38%) exceeded the 28-school-day deadline. Of the open cases, 13 are already overdue. In total, 37.5% of all complaints received to date were or will be late, indicating a recurring issue with timeliness.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Update Report For 2025-2026 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: Adult social care savings projects tracking to miss targets at month 10 of the financial year
findings.detail: The audit of delivery of financial savings in Integrated Adult Social Care found that by month 10 of 2024-25, each of the sampled savings projects was rated as 'unlikely to meet the initial expected financial saving target'. Staff lack readily available data to confirm that actions taken have resulted in savings, making prediction of outcomes difficult.
findings.matters: A lender assesses council financial resilience partly on its ability to deliver planned savings; failure to hit targets signals that budgeted balancing actions are at risk and reserves may face unexpected pressure.
findings.figures: Month 10 2024-25: all sampled projects rated unlikely to meet target
findings.quote: At month 10 2024/25, each of the projects selected was 'delivery confidence rated' as unlikely to meet the initial expected financial saving target.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Update Report For 2025-2026 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: SEND service control weakness from prior year still not resolved, rated No Assurance
findings.detail: The audit of SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disability) services received a No Assurance rating in 2024-25 due to lack of accuracy in data. A follow-up review is underway but not yet concluded. The report states the lack of data accuracy remains the main risk identified.
findings.matters: A No Assurance rating indicates fundamental gaps in control or governance that could expose the council to financial or reputational risk; unresolved data accuracy issues in a statutory service could affect service delivery or financial reporting.
findings.figures: No Assurance rating carried from 2024-25; follow-up results due February 2026
findings.quote: We are in the process of concluding on our follow up review of the previous SEND work where a rating of No Assurance was given, with the main risk identified as a lack of accuracy of the data held by the Service.

findings.paper_title: Devon Pension Fund Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Brunel Pension Partnership deemed unable to meet minimum pooling standards and must be dissolved; Devon Pension Fund must select a replacement provider by 30 September 2025
findings.detail: Following the government's LGPS Fit for the Future consultation outcome in May 2025, Brunel has been identified as unable to meet newly set minimum pooling standards and must dissolve. Devon Pension Fund faces a mandatory transition requiring an 'in principle' decision on which asset pool provider to transfer to within approximately 15 weeks. This is a material forced structural change to how the fund's assets will be managed and administered.
findings.matters: A mandated transition to a new asset pool provider is a significant operational risk event that could affect fund performance, incur transition costs, and disrupt governance continuity—ultimately impacting the fund's financial health and the administering authority's position.
findings.figures: Decision deadline: 30 September 2025
findings.quote: Brunel Pension Partnership has been deemed unable to meet the newly set minimum pooling standards and must therefore be dissolved. The Pension Fund must make an 'in principle' decision as to what provider they will be transferring to, by the end of September 2025.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Stewardship Annual Report 2024-2025 - Cabinet Report
findings.headline: The council refinanced LOBO loans using short-term borrowing from other local authorities rather than fixed-rate debt.
findings.detail: In 2024-25, the council refinanced the remaining LOBO loans (lender option, borrower option loans that had become unfavourable). Rather than take long-term fixed-rate borrowing, the council used £21.5m one-year PWLB borrowing and £35m short-term loans from other councils, betting that rates would fall and it could refinance later at lower cost.
findings.matters: This is a deliberate rate bet: the council believes it is cheaper to wait for lower rates and refinance later, but this leaves it exposed to further rate rises and refinancing risk. Given that rates have already risen since February, this strategy is now looking less favourable.
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing: £21.5m PWLB (1-year) + £35m from other local authorities. Total external debt kept at £507.85m.
findings.quote: Short term borrowing has been used, rather than long term borrowing, on the basis that interest rates were expected to fall, and that long term borrowing would be possible at lower rates in future than those available at the time.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Stewardship Annual Report 2024-2025 - Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Investment income fell £1.86m short of budget because lower cash balances generated fewer returns.
findings.detail: The council earned £5.487m in investment income against a budget of £7.35m. The shortfall is directly attributed to having less cash available to invest; the council's average investment return (4.92%) was close to target, but there was simply less capital to invest.
findings.matters: This is a cascading effect: SEND deficits cut cash, lower cash reduces investment yield, lost yield further pressures the budget. The council is caught in a downward cycle.
findings.figures: Investment income: £5.487m actual vs £7.35m budget (shortfall £1.86m). Average rate 4.92% vs 5% target.
findings.quote: The shortfall against budget can be attributed to the lower than anticipated cash balances available for investment during the year.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Stewardship Annual Report 2024-2025 - Cabinet Report
findings.headline: PWLB borrowing costs have risen sharply since February 2025.
findings.detail: Government borrowing costs available to the council through the Public Works Loans Board have increased across all maturities. The 10-year rate has risen from 5.28% to 5.50%, the 25-year from 5.80% to 6.26%, and the 50-year from 5.51% to 6.02%. The council attributes this to market concerns about inflation and government borrowing levels.
findings.matters: The council was already planning to borrow £50m; the increase in rates will materially increase annual debt service costs. For a lender, this signals the council will face higher financing costs going forward.
findings.quote: The current rates available to the Authority from the Public Works Loans Board (PWLB), compared to those available in February, are shown in the following table.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Stewardship Annual Report 2024-2025 - Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Council must now borrow externally; internal cash can no longer fund the capital programme.
findings.detail: The Treasury Strategy for 2025-26 anticipated £50m of new external borrowing would be needed. The council now confirms it can no longer rely on internal borrowing to fund capital schemes, meaning all future capital works depend on external debt. The council expects to take short-term borrowing before year-end.
findings.matters: Loss of internal funding capacity reduces financial flexibility and increases reliance on external borrowing markets at a time when PWLB rates are rising.
findings.figures: £50 million new external borrowing required; current PWLB 10-year rate 5.50% (up from 5.28% in February); 25-year rate 6.26% (up from 5.80%).
findings.quote: The Authority's reduced levels of cash mean that it is no longer possible to rely on internal borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Stewardship Annual Report 2024-2025 - Cabinet Report
findings.headline: SEND deficit has cut cash reserves by more than half in two years, from £108m to £50m.
findings.detail: The council's cash position has deteriorated sharply. At 31 March 2025, usable cash stood at £50.21m, down from £108.08m two years earlier. The council explicitly attributes this to the Dedicated Schools Grant (SEND) deficit, which continues to drain balances despite a Safety Valve agreement with the Department for Education and £38m received in March 2024.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if cash reserves are sustainable and how much of the decline is structural rather than cyclical; this SEND deficit appears to be an ongoing drain the council cannot easily remedy.
findings.figures: Cash balances: £108.08m (31 March 2023) → £50.21m (31 March 2025). SEND deficit described as 'significantly higher than the cash resources allocated'.
findings.quote: The major reason for the reduction in cash balances is the deficit funding position on Dedicated Schools Grant for Special Educational Needs and Disability (SEND).

findings.committee: Devon and Torbay Combined County Authority Board
findings.paper_title: 250929 - DTCCA Board Report - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitor (Apr-Aug 2025)
findings.headline: Core team budget flexibility depends on £341,279 in interest income and brought-forward balances to manage pressures
findings.detail: The core team's funding includes £72,266 in current-year bank interest and £269,013 brought forward from 2024/25. The authority notes this interest "provides flexibility to help manage budget pressures in both the current and future financial years" and mitigate cashflow impacts.
findings.matters: Financial flexibility is dependent on interest rates and accumulated cash balances. If interest rates fall or balances are depleted, this flexibility diminishes and future budget management options narrow.
findings.figures: £72,266 current year interest; £269,013 brought forward from 2024/25
findings.quote: The interest earned provides flexibility to help manage budget pressures in both the current and future financial years, and to mitigate potential cashflow impacts as operational delivery commences.

findings.committee: Devon and Torbay Combined County Authority Board
findings.paper_title: 250929 - DTCCA Board Report - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitor (Apr-Aug 2025)
findings.headline: Pavement Channels Grant of £377,000 is conditional on application to Department for Transport by 31 October 2025
findings.detail: The authority has been allocated £377,000 through the Pavement Channels Grant, but this requires a formal application to the Department for Transport by 31 October 2025. Delivery will be undertaken by constituent councils on behalf of DTCCA and will be subject to a future report.
findings.matters: This represents conditional capital funding that depends on a successful application by a fixed deadline. Non-compliance would result in loss of this resource.
findings.figures: £377,000 Pavement Channels Grant
findings.quote: In addition, the DTCCA has been allocated £377,000 through the Pavement Channels Grant, subject to a formal application to the Department for Transport by 31 October 2025.

findings.committee: Devon and Torbay Combined County Authority Board
findings.paper_title: 250929 - DTCCA Board Report - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitor (Apr-Aug 2025)
findings.headline: Core team forecast overspend of £21,916 driven by newly commissioned work for Local Transport Authority transition and other programmes
findings.detail: The core team is in £21,916 overspend against full-year budget of £743,720. This is driven by new costs not in the original budget: £26,711 for IT licences for Committee Management System, £1,730 Independent Member Allowances, and newly commissioned work on Local Growth Plan and brand development. The overspend is offset by funding from government capacity grant and interest income.
findings.matters: This shows the organization is taking on new responsibilities and spending scope beyond the approved budget. While offset by funding, it indicates budget expansion that will need to be accommodated in future years.
findings.figures: £21,916 forecast overspend; £26,711 IT licences; £1,730 Independent Member Allowances
findings.quote: The year-end outturn is currently forecast to show an overspend of £21,916 against the full-year budget of £743,720. This variance is largely due to new costs not included in the original budget, including £26,711 for IT licences within support services to implement the DTCCA's Committee Management System, £1,730 for Independent Member Allowances within supplies and services, and the newly commissioned work programmes referenced earlier.

findings.committee: Devon and Torbay Combined County Authority Board
findings.paper_title: 250929 - DTCCA Board Report - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitor (Apr-Aug 2025)
findings.headline: DTCCA to assume Local Transport Authority responsibilities from 1 April 2026 with operational, financial and governance implications yet to be fully assessed
findings.detail: The authority is undertaking preparatory work for a material expansion of scope. An options appraisal assessing operational, financial and governance implications will be presented to the Board in November 2025, with implementation planning to follow before the April 2026 transition. This work is driving current budget overruns.
findings.matters: This represents a major change in the organization's responsibilities and scope that will affect budget requirements, staffing, and operational complexity. A lender needs to understand the financial and operational risk of this transition.
findings.figures: Transition date 1 April 2026
findings.quote: A significant proportion of the current expenditure relates to preparatory work for the DTCCA's future role as the Local Transport Authority. This work, approved by the DTCCA Board at its meeting in July 2025, represents an important step in assessing the operational, financial, and governance implications for DTCCA, Devon County Council, and Torbay Council. The outcomes of this work will be presented as an options appraisal to the DTCCA Board at its next meeting in November 2025

findings.paper_title: Grant Thornton - Devon County Council - Auditors Annual Report for 2024-25 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: No organisational-wide transformation governance in place despite urgent need to deliver £91.5m savings; transformation capability only established May 2025
findings.detail: While the council is developing transformation priorities, there was no overall organisational-wide transformation governance in place during 2024/25. Separate directorate improvement boards operated only for part of the year before reverting to directorate governance. A new Transformation Board and centralised Transformation and Change Team were only established in May 2025. Most savings to date have been identified through directorate-level 'budget sandpit' arrangements rather than organisational transformation.
findings.matters: The absence of structured transformation governance and late establishment of centralised capacity creates execution risk that the council cannot deliver the scale and pace of savings needed to close the structural budget deficit.
findings.figures: Savings gap £91.4m; £23.1m needed 2026/27; transformation governance established May 2025; organisational-wide approach still in early development
findings.quote: While the priority in 2024/25 was to develop the One Council approach, there was no overall organisational wide transformation governance in place. Separate Adults, Children's and Corporate Services Improvement Boards were in place for part of 2024/25 but oversight of savings delivery reverted back to Directorate governance meetings from Autumn 2024. A new Transformation Board is planned to oversee progress against key priorities and benefits realisation, supported by individual Programme Boards. A new centralised Transformation and Change Team has been in place since May 2025.

findings.paper_title: Grant Thornton - Devon County Council - Auditors Annual Report for 2024-25 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: Ofsted rated Children's Services as 'inadequate' in May 2025; internal audit gave limited assurance; multiple control weaknesses identified
findings.detail: Ofsted's May 2025 inspection again rated Children's Services as inadequate (repeated from 2020 assessment). The Head of Internal Audit provided limited assurance for the service in 2024/25 due to findings in SEND traded services, payments to independent placements, placement sufficiency pathway, EHCP payments, and transitions to adulthood. A Local Government Ombudsman Public Interest Report highlighted weaknesses in the pathway for transitioning from children's to adult services.
findings.matters: A second consecutive inadequate Ofsted rating combined with limited internal audit assurance indicates systemic governance and control failures in a service accounting for significant budget growth and overspends, signalling operational risk and potential for escalating costs.
findings.figures: Ofsted rating: inadequate (May 2025, repeated from 2020); internal audit opinion: limited assurance; budget growth 2024/25 £21.5m, 2025/26 £12.4m
findings.quote: Ofsted provided an 'inadequate' assessment of Children's Services in May 2025. Previous joint assessments by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) and Ofsted found significant weaknesses with SEND services In addition, the Head of internal Audit Opinion for 2024/25 provided a 'limited assurance' opinion for Children's services.

findings.paper_title: Grant Thornton - Devon County Council - Auditors Annual Report for 2024-25 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: General Fund balance at 2.3% of budget, well below 5% benchmark, and council ranked last among shire councils for reserve sustainability
findings.detail: The council's General Fund balance of £16m represents only 2.3% of the approved 2025/26 budget of £695.2m, substantially below the benchmark of approximately 5% found in comparable councils. Total GF and earmarked balances have reduced by 36% from £263.4m in 2022 to £167.3m in 2025. The council is ranked last place amongst shire districts for reserve sustainability, level of reserves and change in reserves per the CIPFA financial resilience index.
findings.matters: Low reserves relative to budget size and peer comparison leave the council with minimal buffer for unexpected costs or further budget pressures, creating material financial risk.
findings.figures: GF balance £16m; GF balance as % of budget 2.3%; benchmark typically 5%; total GF and earmarked balances £167.3m (down 36% from £263.4m in 2022); CIPFA ranking last place for shire districts
findings.quote: The level of GF balance at £16m represents only 2.3% of the approved 2025/26 budget requirement of £695.2m, which is lower than in many Councils where the benchmark is closer to 5%. The Council held total GF and earmarked GF balances of £263.4m at 31 March 2022, reducing by 36% to £167.3m by 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Grant Thornton - Devon County Council - Auditors Annual Report for 2024-25 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: Cash position now forces external borrowing; under-borrowed position shrinking from £95.1m to forecast £14.4m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The DSG deficit has directly caused a shift from internal to external borrowing. External borrowing requirement is forecast to increase by £67.7m by 2029/30 to fund the capital programme. Treasury management costs increased by £1m in 2024/25, with £2m reduction in investment income due to lower cash balances. The council's under-borrowed position (available internal resources) is forecast to shrink from £95.1m in 2024/25 to only £14.4m by 2029/30.
findings.matters: This represents a material increase in capital financing costs and a significant reduction in financial flexibility for the council, indicating unsustainability if the DSG statutory override ends in March 2028 as planned.
findings.figures: Cash reduction £50.1m year-on-year; capital financing cost overspend £1m; investment income reduction £2m; forecast external borrowing increase £67.7m by 2029/30; under-borrowed position £95.1m (2024/25) to £14.4m (2029/30)
findings.quote: The financial impact of the reduction in cash balances due to the DSG deficit is clearly reported in Treasury Management reports, with the Council required to externalise borrowing to fund the capital programme rather than utilise internal borrowing, and with less cash available to invest to generate returns. The 2024/25 budget outturn report confirms a £1m overspend on capital financing costs and £2m reduction in interest income as a result of reduced cash balances.

findings.paper_title: Grant Thornton - Devon County Council - Auditors Annual Report for 2024-25 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: Adults and Children's social care combined overspent by £10.4m in 2024/25 despite £49.9m growth allocation and failed to deliver planned savings
findings.detail: Social care services, accounting for 89% of the council's net revenue budget (£620.7m in 25/26), overspent by a combined £10.4m. Adult social care overspent £4.9m despite £49.9m growth; children's services overspent £5.5m despite £30.7m growth. Total savings target was £18.4m, but only £9.8m was delivered (53%). The 2025/26 budget includes further growth totalling £29.1m for adult services alone.
findings.matters: The failure to deliver savings coupled with continued demand and cost pressures in the largest service area represents a structural imbalance that cannot be resolved by growth allocation alone, and signals that assumptions underpinning budget modelling may be unrealistic.
findings.figures: Adult social care budget 89% of net revenue (£620.7m in 25/26); overspend £4.9m; growth £49.9m; children's overspend £5.5m; growth £30.7m; combined overspend £10.4m; savings target £18.4m, delivered £9.8m (53%)
findings.quote: Adults and Children's social care budgets account for the majority of the Council's net revenue budget (£620.7m or 89% in 25/26) and continuing cost and demand pressures on these budgets represent a significant risk to the Council's financial sustainability. The 2024/25 budget included significant growth and pressures relating to these services, although both services overspent at year end by a total of £10.4m due to cost and demand pressures coupled with challenges in delivering agreed savings.

findings.paper_title: Grant Thornton - Devon County Council - Auditors Annual Report for 2024-25 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan requires £91.5m in savings by 2029/30, with £23.1m needed for 2026/27 alone, and only £36.4m currently identified
findings.detail: To balance identified budget gaps, the council requires total savings of £127.8m, of which £36.4m are identified and approved, leaving a gap of £91.4m. The 2026/27 gap is £23.1m. In 2024/25 the council delivered only £40.2m of £49.6m planned savings (81%), a £9.4m shortfall.
findings.matters: The scale of the unidentified savings requirement, combined with demonstrated under-delivery in the prior year, creates material risk that the council cannot balance its budget without service cuts or further reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: Total savings required £127.8m; identified and approved £36.4m; gap £91.4m; 2026/27 gap £23.1m; 2024/25 delivery 81% (£40.2m of £49.6m target); shortfall £9.4m
findings.quote: In order to balance the budget gaps identified in the MTFP, total savings of £127.8m are required, of which £36.4m are currently identified and approved. The remaining gap of £91.4m is a challenging target. The Council did not deliver a significant proportion of planned savings in 2024/25, with net under-delivery of £9.4m (19%), after some mitigations were identified.

findings.paper_title: Grant Thornton - Devon County Council - Auditors Annual Report for 2024-25 - Audit Committee Report
findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit of £169.1m is grossly exceeding the Safety Valve programme trajectory and eroding cash reserves
findings.detail: The annual DSG overspend in 2024/25 was £51.4m against a Safety Valve target of £31.2m. The accumulated deficit reached £169.1m, higher than total useable earmarked reserves of £120.6m. This deficit is the primary driver of a £50.1m (53%) reduction in cash and short-term investments from £94.9m to £44.8m in a single year.
findings.matters: This represents a material erosion of financial resilience and a trajectory breach that forces external borrowing, increasing capital financing costs and reducing investment income—making the council dependent on continuing statutory override protection.
findings.figures: Accumulated DSG deficit £169.1m; 2024/25 overspend £51.4m vs Safety Valve target £31.2m; cash reduction £50.1m (53%); latest 2025/26 projection £53.3m annual deficit vs £10.4m forecast
findings.quote: The Council was not able to meet the Safety Valve targets in 2024/25 due to continuing high demand for EHCPs and independent sector placements. The annual DSG overspend in 2024/25 was £51.4m against the Safety Valve target of £31.2m. This increased the accumulated DSG deficit to £169.1m as at 31 March 2025, with a net deficit of £127.2m after taking into account the Council's contributions of £41.8m held in the Resilience Reserve.
